MIT scientists build a tiny robot that swims using living muscle cells

📅 23 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1493 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, A swimming robot does not necessarily need a bulky motor or powerful mechanical parts to move through water.
  • Industry observers note that the engineers developed an extremely thin swimming robot that uses living muscle tissue to move its fins.
  • According to recent reports, by directing light onto either fin, the researchers can trigger muscle contractions that make the fin flap and push the robot through water.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, A swimming robot does not necessarily need a bulky motor or powerful mechanical parts to move through water. MIT researchers have demonstrated that a single, carefully engineered layer of living muscle cells can generate enough force to propel a tiny robot forward.

Industry observers note that the engineers developed an extremely thin swimming robot that uses living muscle tissue to move its fins. Described in a fresh study published in Advanced Functional Materials, the device has a flexible gel framework roughly the length and width of a stick of gum. The gel forms two fins, each coated with a layer of muscle cells far thinner than a human hair. These cells have been genetically modified to contract when exposed to light.

According to recent reports, by directing light onto either fin, the researchers can trigger muscle contractions that make the fin flap and push the robot through water. Adjusting which fin receives light and how frequently it is illuminated allows the team to control both its speed and direction.

Recent findings suggest that in experiments, the remarkably thin robot successfully swam and turned through a simple underwater maze. At maximum speed, it covered approximately four times its body length per minute. Although that is much slower than an Olympic swimmer, who can travel up to 65 body lengths per minute, it is comparable to the swimming pace of a cow shark moving leisurely through the ocean.

Sources indicate that "It takes a lot of force to move through water versus air," notes study author Ritu Raman, associate professor of mechanical engineering at MIT. "The robot's quite strong, given its size. ".

A Fresh Generation of Robots Powered by Living Muscle.

The device represents the first demonstration of a very thin, two-dimensional robot that can move from place to place using living muscle tissue.

Most existing biohybrid robots rely on relatively large, three-dimensional structures made from laboratory-grown skeletal muscle. Producing these structures typically requires millions of cells. Raman explains that thinner designs could reduce manufacturing costs while potentially improving movement efficiency.

Industry observers note that "At the moment, biohybrid robots from our group and others' are built from bulky, 3D chunks of lab-grown skeletal muscle that require millions of cells to fabricate," indicates Raman, who notes that thinner, less bulky designs such as the team's newly introduced bot could be cheaper to build and could move more efficiently. "We believe that biohybrid robots powered by living muscle could one day perform delicate jobs like exploring environments too fragile or unpredictable for conventional hardware, because living tissue is soft, responsive to its surroundings, and can heal itself.".

The MIT research team also included first author Maheera Bawa, along with Arielle Berman, Laura Schwendeman, Ferdows Afghah, and Seanbiron Johnson.

From Artificial Muscle to a Swimming Robot.

The newly introduced swimming robot builds on an earlier achievement by Raman's laboratory. Last year, the researchers created an artificial muscle disk inspired by the human iris, demonstrating how a thin layer of living cells could produce precisely controlled movements.

In a recent development, for that project, the engineers patterned a gel disk with grooves extending outward from its center and forming concentric circles. They then placed living muscle cells on the surface, where the cells grew into a thin layer following the patterned channels.

Sources indicate that when illuminated, the muscle tissue contracted in different directions, causing the disk to stretch and compress. Its movements resembled the way the iris of the human eye changes shape as the pupil expands or narrows.

The experiment established that researchers could grow extremely thin muscle layers in intricate arrangements and use light to control their movements along multiple directions.

In a recent development, "People hadn't seen this muscle architecture engineered from scratch before," Raman notes. "And the cells were moving in multiple directions. But they only moved about 100 microns. From a robotics perspective, their movements were tiny.".

For the latest project, the researchers wanted to dramatically increase the amount of movement and force generated by the muscle cells. Their goal was to produce contractions powerful enough to propel a robot through water.

They determined that achieving this would require a better foundation for the living muscle tissue.

The earlier artificial iris had used fibrin, an exceptionally soft gel, as its underlying structure. However, the team found that fibrin could promptly shrink under the forces exerted by contracting muscle cells, limiting the effectiveness of the resulting movement.

To overcome this problem, the engineers investigated three characteristics of the gel foundation: its chemical composition, its stiffness, and the dimensions and geometry of the grooves used to organize muscle growth.

"For engineering any type of tissue, it's known that these are knobs you can tune," Raman states. "And we wanted to optimize all these parameters to support live muscle cells.".

Engineering a Stronger Muscle-Powered Robot.

Finding the right supporting material required testing gels with different formulations, stiffness levels, and surface patterns.

It has been revealed that the researchers compared several groove shapes, including narrow channels with square profiles and longer channels with curved bottoms. They discovered that muscle cells aligned more effectively inside square-shaped grooves.

According to recent reports, this alignment was vital because muscle cells that grow in the same direction are more likely to merge into fibers. Those fibers can then form stronger muscle tissue that contracts in a coordinated way. The square grooves therefore provided a more effective structure for producing force.

The team also replaced fibrin with gelatin methacrylate (GelMA), a material commonly used to grow and engineer biological tissue.

It has been revealed that by adjusting the formulation of GelMA, the researchers produced supporting gels with varying degrees of stiffness. They then examined how muscle cells developed on each surface and measured their ability to generate force.

Stiffer gels produced the best results. On these firmer surfaces, muscle cells grew in better alignment and generated stronger contractions.

The engineers next investigated how thick the gel should be. They determined that a film measuring approximately half a millimeter offered an effective balance. It was sturdy enough to support a single layer of muscle cells while remaining sufficiently lightweight to prevent the contracting cells from detaching from the surface.

The team further improved muscle performance through a form of exercise. Repeated pulses of light stimulated the cells to contract, strengthening the muscle tissue before it was incorporated into the swimming robot.

How Light Makes the Living Robot Swim.

With the gel structure optimized and the muscle cells strengthened, the researchers assembled their swimming device.

Recent findings suggest that the finished robot consisted of a thin gel framework divided into two fins. Both sides of the gel were patterned with square-bottomed grooves and covered with living muscle cells. As the cells developed, they fused into organized muscle fibers capable of contracting together.

Each fin could be activated independently using light, giving the researchers a simple way to control the robot's movements.

"You can think of the robot as having two independent muscles," Raman says. "If we shine a light on just one, only that muscle moves. If shining on both, they both flap.".

Recent findings suggest that to test the device, the researchers placed it inside a large petri dish filled with water. They then moved a light source by hand, illuminating the fins to guide the robot through a maze positioned inside the dish.

In a recent development, as the muscles contracted, the fins flapped and propelled the robot through the water. By changing the light stimulation, the engineers successfully controlled its movement and helped it navigate the obstacles.

Recent findings suggest that although the robot demonstrated the ability to swim and steer, its current shape remains relatively simple. The primary objective of the experiment was to establish that an exceptionally thin layer of engineered muscle tissue could generate enough force for swimming.

The researchers now initiative to refine the robot's body to improve its speed. Beyond demonstrating a upcoming approach to biohybrid robotics, the technology could eventually be useful for monitoring aquatic environments or operating in locations where conventional rigid machines might cause damage.

In a recent development, "Our next goal is to optimize the body design to enable faster swimming," Raman says. "But even at slow swim speeds, one could imagine a muscle-powered swimmer being used for purposes like environmental monitoring in aquatic environments.".

The Office of Naval Research provided partial funding for this research.

Visual Salamandra: Pushing the Boundaries of Multimodal Understanding

📅 11 Apr 2025 | ⏱️ 4 min read (778 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The Language Technologies Lab takes a major step forward in multimodal artificial intelligence with the release of Visual Salamandra, extending the capabilities of the Salamandra large language model (LLM) to both images and video.
  • Designed with vision-language alignment at its core, Visual Salamandra builds on top of the Salamandra Instructed 7B model by integrating Google’s SigLIP encoder (SigLIP-So400m), a 2-layer MLP projector, and advanced late-fusion techniques to bridge the gap between visual and textual modalities.
  • The resulting architecture enables Visual Salamandra to comprehend and generate contextually accurate responses from diverse inputs, ranging from single and multiple images and videos to purely textual instructions.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Language Technologies Lab takes a major step forward in multimodal artificial intelligence with the release of Visual Salamandra, extending the capabilities of the Salamandra large language model (LLM) to both images and video. Visual Salamandra is based on the 7 billion parameters foundational model maintaining its compactness and efficiency while extending it to multimodal tasks.

Designed with vision-language alignment at its core, Visual Salamandra builds on top of the Salamandra Instructed 7B model by integrating Google’s SigLIP encoder (SigLIP-So400m), a 2-layer MLP projector, and advanced late-fusion techniques to bridge the gap between visual and textual modalities.

The resulting architecture enables Visual Salamandra to comprehend and generate contextually accurate responses from diverse inputs, ranging from single and multiple images and videos to purely textual instructions. This development reflects a broader commitment by the Lab to support robust, multilingual, and multimodal AI systems—especially those that prioritize European linguistic diversity.

To adapt Salamandra for visual inputs, the Lab implemented a four-phase training process centered on late-fusion architecture. In this setup, a pre-trained image encoder (SigLIP, 14 patches at 384x384 resolution) generates image embeddings, which are then aligned with the LLM via a custom-trained multilayer perceptron (MLP) projector.

The four training phases include:.

• Phase 1: Projector Pre-training – Only the projector is trained to map image features into the LLM’s latent space.

• Phase 2: High-Quality Vision Pretraining – Using refined datasets (e.g., OCR and re-captioned images), the entire architecture (encoder, projector, and LLM) undergoes joint training.

• Phase 3: Instruction Tuning – The model learns to follow user instructions via visual question answering (VQA), OCR, and other grounded vision tasks.

• Phase 4: Full Multimodal Tuning – Incorporates single/multi-image and video data, along with text-only examples, to optimize the model’s generalization to real-world, multi-input scenarios.

Data diversity played a crucial role throughout training. A total of 6.1 million instruction-tuning instances were used, including 842,000 text-only samples. The training corpus featured data from sources like AI2D, Cambrian, and LLaVA Next, chosen to enhance visual grounding, document understanding, mathematical reasoning, and OCR.

Industry observers note that figure 1. Data distribution during the Visual Salamandra 7B training process.

As with previous models from the Language Technologies Lab, Visual Salamandra continues the commitment to multilingual inclusivity, with a strong focus on European languages.

Sources indicate that this approach guarantees that underrepresented languages benefit from instruction tuning and alignment with vision tasks, helping to close the resource gap in multimodal AI research. Visual Salamandra is one of the first models of its kind to integrate such linguistic plurality into a multimodal instruction-tuned framework.

Figure 2. Multilingual generation examples with the model trained with Text Regularization and merged with the original backbone LLM.

Visual Salamandra unlocks a wide range of applications at the intersection of language and vision, such as:.

• Visual Question Answering (VQA): Ask questions about an image or video and receive context-aware, accurate responses.

• Optical Character Recognition (OCR): Accurately read and transcribe text from documents, scenes, and charts.

• Document and Chart Understanding: Analyze complex visual documents or graphical content with embedded text.

• Mathematical Reasoning: Solve visually grounded math problems through multimodal reasoning.

• Instruction-based Image Interaction: Follow detailed instructions in visual contexts, including image captioning and localization tasks.

The inclusion of video capabilities also opens the door for further developments in video summarization, event detection, and multimodal storytelling...

Industry observers note that with Visual Salamandra, the Language Technologies Lab demonstrates its ongoing leadership in creating inclusive, high-performing foundational models. By harmonizing state-of-the-art vision encoders with strong multilingual LLMs, the team is setting the stage for next-generation AI systems that see, understand, and communicate—across modalities and languages.

While Visual Salamandra reveals strong multimodal capabilities, it is crucial to note its limitations:.

• It may hallucinate plausible but incorrect answers, especially when visual inputs are ambiguous.

• Performance on complex OCR and dense document layouts is still challenging.

• The model was trained with filtered and licensed datasets, but people should remain vigilant about potential biases or inaccuracies, particularly when deployed in sensitive applications.

We recommend using Visual Salamandra in contexts where human oversight is possible and avoiding high-stakes applications without proper evaluation.

Visual Salamandra is released under a Apache License, Version 2.0, allowing for research and non-commercial use.

Stay tunned for future releases and tools built on Visual Salamandra, and explore the full model details in our paper.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • A latest optical sensor costing just $10 could bring laboratory-level precision to wearable health monitors, potentially allowing people to track blood glucose without needles.
  • In a recent development, researchers at the University of Cambridge and GlitterinTech (a start-up founded by the same research group) have developed a latest type of optical spectrometer that combines exceptional accuracy with a remarkably small size and low cost.
  • Optical spectrometers work by analyzing light to reveal information about the substances it interacts with.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A latest optical sensor costing just $10 could bring laboratory-level precision to wearable health monitors, potentially allowing people to track blood glucose without needles. The technology could also transform food testing, industrial quality control, and environmental monitoring.

In a recent development, researchers at the University of Cambridge and GlitterinTech (a start-up founded by the same research group) have developed a latest type of optical spectrometer that combines exceptional accuracy with a remarkably small size and low cost. Measuring just centimeters across, the device could be incorporated into portable electronics and wearable health technology. Its potential applications range from monitoring important health markers in real time to identifying materials and detecting changes in chemical composition.

Optical spectrometers work by analyzing light to reveal information about the substances it interacts with. They are essential tools in medicine, manufacturing, chemical testing, and environmental research. However, making these instruments smaller has traditionally meant compromising their performance. Compact spectrometers often have limited measurement ranges, reduced resolution, or lower accuracy, making them better suited to identifying substances than performing precise measurements.

In a recent development, the researchers believe their latest design could overcome these limitations. Known as a convolutional spectrometer, it uses a mathematical principle called the convolution theorem to analyze light in a fundamentally different way. According to the team, this approach delivers performance that surpasses existing types of spectrometers in several key areas, including designs based on light dispersion, Fourier transforms, and computational reconstruction.

A New Way to Analyze Light With Extraordinary Precision.

Traditional spectrometers generally separate incoming light into its component wavelengths or use complex calculations to reconstruct its spectrum. The new device takes another approach by performing a mathematical operation called convolution directly on the incoming light.

Recent findings suggest that to accomplish this, the researchers arranged optical components with repeating spectral responses in a sequence. These components can include unbalanced Mach-Zehnder interferometers or micro-ring resonators. By adjusting them in proportion to one another, the system can shift its response to different wavelengths in a controlled, linear fashion. Fast Fourier transforms are then used to accurately recover the light spectrum.

Sources indicate that "The key insight was to go back to the mathematics and ask whether there was a fundamentally cleaner way to retrieve spectra," noted Dr. Chunhui Yao, a lead author of the study. "By using the convolution theorem directly in the optical domain, we avoid many of the limitations that have held miniaturized spectrometers back. This gives us high precision, strong noise tolerance, and very low computational overhead, all in a compact and low-cost system.".

The researchers built the spectrometer using a silicon nitride photonic platform and integrated it with onboard electronics. It operates across a broad range of near-infrared wavelengths (1200-1700 nm) and can collect and process measurements in less than a second.

Recent findings suggest that another key advantage is its ability to expand its measurement capabilities without major hardware changes. Because the system uses repeating optical patterns, its spectral bandwidth can theoretically be extended almost without limit. Adding more optical components in sequence can also increase its resolution exponentially.

A $10 Sensor That Could Transform Food Testing and Healthcare.

To evaluate the device outside purely theoretical measurements, the researchers tested it on a variety of materials and substances. The results demonstrated its potential for applications that normally depend on larger, more expensive laboratory instruments.

When used to identify plastics, pharmaceuticals, coffee, flour, and tea, the spectrometer achieved a 100% classification success rate in the reported tests. It also measured concentrations in water-based and organic solutions with accuracies of approximately 0.01%, exceeding the performance of commercial benchtop spectrometers in those experiments.

The healthcare demonstrations were particularly promising. Under conditions designed to reflect real physiological environments, the device accurately measured several human biomarkers, including skin moisture, blood alcohol, blood lactate, and blood glucose.

According to recent reports, the researchers also demonstrated noninvasive glucose tracking over an extended period in one participant. Although further testing would be needed before the technology could become a practical medical product, the finding suggests a possible route toward monitoring blood sugar without repeatedly piercing the skin.

"These biomedical demonstrations are particularly exciting," noted Prof. Qixiang Cheng, who led the project. "What makes this work stand out is not just performance in the lab, but technical readiness. Dr. Chunhui Yao's contribution was crucial in translating a mathematical concept into a fully packaged, robust system that operates reliably across temperature extremes and real-world conditions. That combination is what opens the door to practical deployment.".

The sensor also demonstrated impressive resistance to temperature changes. It continued operating reliably between -20°C and 80°C, an unusually wide temperature range for a miniature spectrometer. This durability could be especially valuable for wearable devices, factory equipment, and sensors operating outdoors.

Why a Simpler Design Could Be a Major Breakthrough.

Recent findings suggest that the fresh spectrometer's advantages extend beyond its accuracy, size, and price. Its internal design also reduces the amount of computing power needed to analyze incoming light.

Many existing miniature spectrometers depend on complicated calibration procedures and demanding algorithms to reconstruct spectral information. These methods can become unreliable when measurements contain noise, and they often require substantial processing resources.

It has been revealed that the Cambridge team's convolution-based approach avoids much of this complexity. Because the measurements follow a linear mathematical relationship, the system can recover spectra rapidly and consistently while using relatively little computational power.

Industry observers note that "This is a beautiful example of how elegant engineering can unlock real impact," said Prof. Richard Penty, who contributed to the photonic system design and integration. "The architecture is simple, scalable, and manufacturable, yet it delivers precision that rivals or exceeds much larger instruments. Dr. Chunhui Yao played a central role in bringing together the photonic design, system integration, and experimental validation that made this possible.".

Its relatively simple construction could also make the technology easier to manufacture on a large scale, potentially bringing sophisticated optical measurements to devices where conventional spectrometers would be too bulky or expensive.

Bringing Laboratory-Grade Measurements to Everyday Devices.

The researchers envision a future in which accurate optical sensing becomes a routine feature of everyday technology rather than something largely confined to specialized laboratories.

In industrial settings, inexpensive spectrometers could be installed throughout manufacturing facilities to continuously check material composition and product quality. Similar sensors could monitor food freshness, identify substances, and analyze environmental conditions on a much larger scale than is at the moment practical.

Sources indicate that healthcare could see equally significant changes. Compact sensors might eventually enable wearables to measure hydration levels, detect signs of alcohol intoxication, track biomarkers related to physical fitness, or continuously monitor glucose levels for people managing diabetes.

Industry observers note that "Our vision is to make spectrometry as ubiquitous as temperature or motion sensing," added Prof. Qixiang Cheng. "This work demonstrates that high-quality spectral information doesn't have to be confined to the laboratory -- it can be embedded directly into the technologies people use every day.".

Sources indicate that as photonic technology becomes smaller and more advanced, the convolutional spectrometer provides a promising example of how mathematical insights and practical engineering can make sophisticated scientific instruments simpler, cheaper, and more accessible. By combining high precision with a device that costs around $10, the researchers have opened a potential path toward a latest generation of smart sensors capable of measuring the hidden chemistry of our bodies and surroundings.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that hugging Face and Protect AI partnered in October 2024 to enhance machine learning (ML) model security through Guardian’s scanning technology for the community of developers who explore and use models from the Hugging Face Hub.
  • Since October, Protect AI has significantly expanded Guardian's detection capabilities, improving existing threat detection capabilities and launching four new detection modules:.
  • Industry observers note that with these updates, Guardian covers more model file formats and detects additional sophisticated obfuscation techniques, including the high severity CVE-2025-1550 vulnerability in Keras.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that hugging Face and Protect AI partnered in October 2024 to enhance machine learning (ML) model security through Guardian’s scanning technology for the community of developers who explore and use models from the Hugging Face Hub. The partnership has been a natural fit from the start—Hugging Face is on a mission to democratize the use of open source AI, with a commitment to safety and security; and Protect AI is building the guardrails to make open source models safe for all.

Since October, Protect AI has significantly expanded Guardian's detection capabilities, improving existing threat detection capabilities and launching four new detection modules:.

Industry observers note that with these updates, Guardian covers more model file formats and detects additional sophisticated obfuscation techniques, including the high severity CVE-2025-1550 vulnerability in Keras. Through enhanced detection tooling, Hugging Face customers receive critical security information via inline alerts on the platform and gain access to comprehensive vulnerability reports on Insights DB. Clearly labeled findings are available on each model page, empowering users to make more informed decisions about which models to integrate into their projects.

As of April 1, 2025, Protect AI has successfully scanned 4.47 million unique model versions in 1.41 million repositories on the Hugging Face Hub.

In a recent development, to date, Protect AI has identified a total of 352,000 unsafe/suspicious issues across 51,700 models. In just the last 30 days, Protect AI has served 226 million requests from Hugging Face at a 7.94 ms response time.

Protect AI’s Guardian applies a zero trust approach to AI/ML security. This especially comes into play when treating arbitrary code execution as inherently unsafe, regardless of intent. Rather than just classifying overtly malicious threats, Guardian flags execution risks as suspicious on InsightsDB, recognizing that even harmful code can look innocuous through obfuscation techniques (see more on payload obfuscation below). Attackers can disguise payloads within seemingly benign scripts or extensibility components of a framework, making payload inspection alone insufficient for ensuring security. By maintaining this cautious approach, Guardian helps mitigate risks posed by hidden threats in machine learning models.

AI/ML security threats are evolving every single day. That's why Protect AI leverages both in-house threat research teams and huntr—the world's first and largest AI/ML bug bounty program powered by our community of over 17,000 security researchers.

According to recent reports, coinciding with our partnership launch in October, Protect AI rolled out a fresh program on huntr to crowdsource research on new Model File Vulnerabilities. Since the launch of the program, they have received over 200 reports that Protect AI teams have worked through and incorporated into Guardian—all of which are automatically applied to the model scans here on Hugging Face.

As more huntr reports come in and more independent threat research is conducted, certain trends have emerged.

In a recent development, library-dependent attack chains: These attacks focus on a bad actor’s ability to invoke functions from libraries present in the ML workstations environment. These are reminiscent of the “drive-by download” style of attacks that afflicted browsers and systems when common utilities like Java and Flash were present. Typically, the scale of impact of these attacks are proportional to the pervasiveness of a given library, with common ML libraries like Pytorch having a far wider potential impact than lesser used libraries.

It has been revealed that payload obfuscation: Several reports have highlighted ways to insert, obfuscate, or “hide” a payload in a model that bypasses common scanning techniques. These vulnerabilities use techniques like compression, encoding, and serialization to obfuscate the payload and are not easily detectable. Compression is an matter since libraries like Joblib allow compressed payloads to be loaded directly. Container formats like Keras and NeMo embed additional model files, each potentially vulnerable to their own specific attack vectors. Compression exposes users to TarSlip or ZipSlip vulnerabilities. While the impacts of these will often be limited to Denial of Service, in certain circumstances these vulnerabilities can lead to Arbitrary Code Execution by leveraging path traversal techniques, allowing malicious attackers to overwrite files that are often automatically executed.

Framework-extensibility vulnerabilities: ML frameworks provide numerous extensibility mechanisms that inadvertently create dangerous attack vectors: custom layers, external code dependencies, and configuration-based code loading. For example, CVE-2025-1550 in Keras, reported to us by the huntr community, demonstrates how custom layers can be exploited to execute arbitrary code despite security features. Configuration files with serialization vulnerabilities similarly allow dynamic code loading. These deserialization vulnerabilities make models exploitable through crafted payloads embedded in formats that users load without suspicion. Despite security improvements from vendors, older vulnerable versions and insecure dependency handling continue to present significant risk in ML ecosystems.

Attack vector chaining: Recent reports demonstrate how multiple vulnerabilities can be combined to create sophisticated attack chains that can bypass detection. By sequentially exploiting vulnerabilities like obfuscated payloads and extension mechanisms, researchers have shown complex pathways for compromise that appear benign when examined individually. This approach significantly complicates detection and mitigation efforts, as security tools focused on single-vector threats often miss these compound attacks. Effective defense requires identifying and addressing all links in the attack chain rather than treating each vulnerability in isolation.

The industry-leading Protect AI threat research team, with help from the huntr community, is continuously gathering data and insights in order to develop upcoming and more robust model scans as well as automatic threat blocking (available to Guardian customers). In the last few months, Guardian has:.

According to recent reports, enhanced detection of library-dependent attacks: Significant expansion of Guardian’s scanning capabilities for detecting library-dependent attack vectors. The scanners for PyTorch and Pickle now perform deep structure analysis of serialized code, examining execution paths and identifying potentially malicious code patterns that could be triggered through library dependencies. For example, the PyTorch torchvision.io functions can overwrite any file on the victim’s system to either include a payload or delete all of its content. Guardian can now detect many more of these dangerous functions in popular libraries such as PyTorch, Numpy, and Pandas.

Uncovered obfuscated attacks: Guardian performs multi-layered analyses across various archive formats, decompressing nested archives and examining compressed payloads for malicious models. This approach detects attempts to hide malicious code through compression, encoding, or serialization techniques. Joblib, for example, supports saving models using different compression formats which can obfuscate Pickle deserialization vulnerabilities, and the same can be done in other formats like Keras which can include Numpy weights files that have deserialization payloads in them.

Detected exploits in framework extensibility components: Guardian’s constantly improving detection modules alerted customers on Hugging Face to models that were impacted by CVE-2025-1550 (a critical security finding) before the vulnerability was publicly disclosed. These detection modules comprehensively analyze ML framework extension mechanisms, allowing only standard or verified components and blocking potentially dangerous implementations, regardless of their apparent intent.

Identified additional architectural backdoors: Guardian’s architectural backdoor detection capabilities were expanded beyond ONNX formats to include additional model formats like TensorFlow.

Expanded model format coverage: Guardian’s true strength comes from the depth of its coverage, which has driven substantial expansion of detection modules to include additional formats like Joblib and an increasingly popular llamafile format, with support for additional ML frameworks coming soon.

Recent findings suggest that provided deeper model analysis: Actively research on additional ways to augment current detection capabilities for better analysis and detection of unsafe models. Expect to see significant enhancements in reducing both false positives and false negatives in the near future.

Industry observers note that through the partnership with Protect AI and Hugging Face, we’ve made third-party ML models safer and more accessible. We believe that having more eyes on model security can only be a good thing. We’re increasingly seeing the security world pay attention and lean in, making threats more discoverable and AI usage safer for all.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Simon Alibert and Rémi Cadène from the LeRobot team with Reachy 1 — Photo: Léa Crespi.

Since Hugging Face started the LeRobot library in 2024, led by ex-Tesla lead Remi Cadene, the Hugging Face Hub has quickly become the most widely used hub and software platform for open robotics with models, datasets, spaces and libraries.

Today, we’re excited to take it a step further by welcoming Pollen Robotics to Hugging Face, a team that's spent the last 9 years building open-source robots and hardware.

It has been revealed that we believe robotics could be the next frontier unlocked by AI — and it should be open, affordable, and private. Our vision: a future where everyone in the community, from hobbyists to enterprises, can build or use robot assistants or games, starting from open solutions instead of closed, remote controlled, hardware.

From the start, we built Pollen Robotics with open source at its core, driven by our belief that robots will play a profound role in our lives — serving as the interface between AI and the physical world. Hugging Face is a natural home for us to grow, as we share a common goal: putting AI and robotics in the hands of everyone.

This marks the fifth acquisition for Hugging Face, after notable additions like Gradio and XetHub.

According to Clem's 2025 prediction about robots, "at least 100k personal robots will be pre-ordered" this year, signaling massive growth in the space.

This month also celebrates one year since Hugging Face created LeRobot. The community of LeRobot-native DIY robot builders has flourished on YouTube and Discord, truly democratizing access to robotics technology. In just twelve months, the GitHub repository has grown from zero to over 12,000 stars, with dramatic growth continuing into 2025.

In a recent development, the first robot we’re offering is Reachy 2 — your friendly little lab partner for the AI era that is already in use in labs like Cornell or Carnegie Mellon. It’s a state-of-the-art humanoid robot that is open-source & VR-compatible, built for research, education, and embodied AI experiments. You can already order one for $70,000 by emailing sales@pollen-robotics.com.

Sources indicate that hugging Face is the most used platform for AI builders, with over 7 million people and a thriving community of researchers, developers, and organizations. Founded by Clément Delangue (CEO), Julien Chaumond (CTO), and Thomas Wolf (CSO), the organization has become a central hub for AI, hosting the most popular open-source models and datasets, including Meta’s LLaMA 4, DeepSeek R1, Stable Diffusion, Black Forest Flux, Mistral, OpenAI Whisper and millions of others. Its AI app store features over 500,000 ready-to-use applications called spaces, making state-of-the-art AI accessible to all. Hugging Face has raised over $395 million to date from leading investors including Google, Amazon, Nvidia, Salesforce, Sequoia, Coatue, Lux Capital, and Addition.

In a recent development, pollen Robotics, established in 2016, is a leading developer of open-source humanoid robots designed for advanced research and real-world applications. Founded by former researchers from Inria's Flowers team, including Matthieu Lapeyre and Pierre Rouanet, the tech giant leverages years of experience at the intersection of robotics hardware and applied artificial intelligence, to develop innovative and user-friendly robotic platforms. Reachy 2 is the latest generation of Pollen Robotics’ flagship humanoid robot. Designed as a versatile platform for embodied AI, Reachy 2 combines advanced hardware with user-friendly software, enabling intuitive interactions and agile manipulation. With open-source hardware and software at its core, Reachy 2 provides researchers, and developers unprecedented freedom to explore human-robot interactions, machine learning applications, and practical AI-driven tasks.

Reachy has been adopted by esteemed institutions such as Accenture, CEA, CNRS, Cornell University, and Carnegie Mellon University, underscoring its versatility in fields ranging from advanced AI research to practical manipulation tasks. Pollen Robotics has won several awards including second place at the prestigious ANA Avatar XPRIZE in 2022, highlighting its innovative prowess in remote presence, dexterous manipulation and control technologies.

With hundreds of units deployed across more than 20 countries, Pollen Robotics has redefined the capabilities of open-source humanoid robots, fostering collaboration and customization in the global robotics community.

7 Day Free Trial. Cancel Anytime.

Here is a question a product page should answer in about five seconds: “Will this magnetic phone mount hold my phone with the case still on?” When the answer is hard to find, shoppers tend to open another tab instead of contacting support.

Stores that sell both car accessories and home & kitchen products face an extra challenge: two very different catalogs share one site. A car accessories buyer cares about fit, mounting and compatibility. A home & kitchen buyer cares about size, capacity and how easy the product is to clean. A single generic product page frustrates both.

This guide covers seven practical e-commerce UX tips that designers and developers can apply right away, with code snippets and a checklist at the end.

In a recent development, A car mount and a vegetable peeler should not share the same spec table. Keep a single reusable product page component and change only the fields based on category. The layout stays consistent, while each shopper sees the details they need.

In code, this can be a config object that your template reads from:.

Showing “Not specified” instead of hiding a missing field is a small habit with a real benefit: it makes gaps in your product data visible to your own team.

Shoppers look for deal-breaker information near the price and the purchase button: fit, size and compatibility. Do not bury it in an “Additional information” tab halfway down the page.

According to recent reports, A short comparison table also works better than three paragraphs of marketing copy, because shoppers scan rather than read. Baymard Institute’s product page research consistently finds that unclear or hard-to-find specifications are a common reason shoppers hesitate.

A responsive layout is the starting point, not the finish line. People compare car accessories in a parking lot and browse kitchen gadgets while standing in the kitchen, often with one thumb.

Recent findings suggest that A phone mount on a white background claims nothing about how it attaches to a dashboard. Show it in a real car, from the driver’s point of view. For home & kitchen products, place the item next to something familiar, like a coffee mug, so people can judge its size.

Good alt text matters for accessibility and for image search. Compare “phone mount” with “Magnetic phone mount fixed to a car dashboard, holding a phone in landscape mode”. The W3C alt text decision tree is a useful guide for deciding what to describe.

It has been revealed that keep images fast, too. Responsive sources with srcset and sizes, explicit dimensions and lazy loading help prevent layout shift and slow pages:.

One caveat: do not lazy-load the main product image at the top of the page. It is usually the Largest Contentful Paint element, so web.dev advises loading it eagerly.

Shoppers often search for a problem rather than a product. Few people type “seat gap filler” the first time; they type “stuff falling between car seats”. Your search, synonyms and category names should handle both.

In a recent development, mixed catalogs show why this matters. Stores that cover both vehicle and household products, such as VNSPORT.org with its separate product collections, keep the two audiences apart so that someone looking for a dashboard mount never has to scroll past kitchen tools. The principle applies to any store with more than one audience: group by the shopper’s intent, not by your supplier list.

Decorative “100% secure” badges do little. What builds trust is information shoppers can check for themselves:.

According to recent reports, at checkout, show the full cost, including shipping and taxes, before payment, let people fix mistakes easily and offer guest checkout. In Baymard’s checkout usability research, unexpected extra costs and forced account creation are among the top reasons shoppers abandon a cart.

According to recent reports, if your support inbox gets the same question every week, the product page has a gap. Answer it on the page, close to where the decision happens, instead of on a generic help page three clicks away.

You can mark up those answers with FAQPage structured data:.

Scientists overcome a hidden obstacle to more powerful quantum computers

📅 26 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (991 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, silicon spin qubits could play a major role in the future of quantum computing because they can be produced using the same semiconductor manufacturing methods that make today's computer chips.
  • Industry observers note that researchers at the RIKEN Center for Emergent Matter Science and their collaborators have now made key progress toward solving this problem.
  • Leon Camenzind, a RIKEN research scientist and co-first author who supervised the experiments, explains the significance of the results: "This shows that high-fidelity control can be maintained even when several qubits are operated at the same time and represents an key step toward scaling up silicon-based quantum processors.".
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, silicon spin qubits could play a major role in the future of quantum computing because they can be produced using the same semiconductor manufacturing methods that make today's computer chips. However, researchers have faced a significant challenge. When multiple silicon qubits are controlled at the same time, their operations tend to become less accurate. Building practical, large quantum computers will require scientists to control many qubits simultaneously while keeping errors to a minimum.

Industry observers note that researchers at the RIKEN Center for Emergent Matter Science and their collaborators have now made key progress toward solving this problem. In a study published in Nature Physics, the team demonstrated highly accurate control of several silicon spin qubits operating simultaneously. Their experiments used an array of five qubits connected to a shared microwave control line. By identifying a major cause of errors during simultaneous operation, the scientists developed a technique to reduce those errors and maintain precision.

Leon Camenzind, a RIKEN research scientist and co-first author who supervised the experiments, explains the significance of the results: "This shows that high-fidelity control can be maintained even when several qubits are operated at the same time and represents an key step toward scaling up silicon-based quantum processors.".

Scientists Identify a Hidden Source of Quantum Computing Errors.

Unlike conventional computers, which store information as bits representing either 0 or 1, quantum computers use quantum bits, or qubits, that can exist in combinations of both states. Silicon spin qubits store this information using the spin of individual electrons confined within silicon. Performing reliable quantum calculations requires extremely precise control over these electron spins.

It has been revealed that microwave signals provide that control, but operating multiple qubits simultaneously can create unwanted effects that interfere with their accuracy. The researchers traced much of this problem to a phenomenon called the AC Stark shift.

This effect occurs when microwave control signals alter a qubit's effective energy levels, producing changes in the phase of its quantum state. Those phase shifts can disrupt the intended operation of individual qubits, particularly when several are being controlled at once.

According to recent reports, to counteract the problem, the team created a calibration method that compensates for these unwanted shifts. Rather than separately calibrating every possible combination of qubits, the technique relies on calibrations performed between pairs of qubits. This makes the approach more practical for systems containing larger numbers of quantum bits.

"Rather than requiring an entirely separate calibration procedure for every possible combination of qubits, our method uses calibrations between pairs of qubits to compensate for the unwanted phase shifts," explains Yi-Hsien Wu, the first author who carried out the experiments as part of his PhD research.

Quantum Qubits Achieve Accuracy Above 99.99%.

It has been revealed that the researchers combined their calibration technique with an improved device design and carefully adjusted microwave control pulses. Their results highlighted that exceptionally high accuracy could be maintained even when multiple qubits were operating simultaneously.

In a recent development, when the five qubits were tested individually, each achieved single-qubit gate fidelity well above 99.99%, with the highest approaching 99.999%. Fidelity describes how closely a quantum operation matches its intended result.

The team then tested how well the system performed when several qubits were active together. With as many as three qubits operating simultaneously, fidelity remained above 99.99%. Even when all five qubits were controlled at once, accuracy stayed at approximately 99.9%, approaching the levels needed for practical fault-tolerant quantum computing.

Although the calibration method greatly reduced errors, it did not eliminate them entirely. The researchers found that the remaining loss of accuracy was linked to drive-induced decoherence, an effect caused by the greater microwave power required to operate multiple qubits simultaneously.

Unlike the unwanted phase shifts corrected by the newly introduced technique, decoherence involves the loss of the delicate quantum coherence needed for reliable operations.

According to Camenzind, "This is a limitation, but further improvements to device design could help mitigate this source of error.".

A New Path Toward Larger Quantum Processors.

Sources indicate that the findings show that controlling several silicon spin qubits at the same time does not necessarily require a major sacrifice in accuracy. By correcting a key source of errors, the researchers have demonstrated a promising approach for operating more qubits through shared microwave control lines.

This is especially important for the development of large quantum processors. Giving every qubit its own independent control system would make increasingly complex devices difficult to manage. Shared control lines could offer a more practical way to expand these systems while maintaining the precision needed for quantum calculations.

"By addressing a key source of control errors through pairwise calibration," says Camenzind. "Our study supports the use of shared control lines as a practical approach to scaling up quantum processors. Combined with silicon's compatibility with established semiconductor manufacturing, we believe that this advance could help pave the way toward larger quantum processors capable of performing increasingly complex computations.".

It has been revealed that the broader objective is to develop quantum computers that can reliably perform calculations despite the errors and disturbances that affect quantum systems. Such machines, known as fault-tolerant quantum computers, will require precise, dependable control over large numbers of qubits.

"Our long-term goal is to build a fault-tolerant quantum computer based on silicon spin qubits, and reliable parallel control is an essential step toward that goal," adds Seigo Tarucha, project manager of a silicon quantum computing project under JST's Moonshot Goal 6.

Introducing HELMET: Holistically Evaluating Long-context Language Models

📅 16 Apr 2025 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1740 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Contact: hyen@cs.princeton.edu Paper: https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.02694 Website: https://princeton-nlp.github.io/HELMET Code & Data: https://github.com/princeton-nlp/HELMET.
  • Since we first released HELMET last October, there has been more development on long-context language models than ever before, and we are thrilled to see the adoption of HELMET by the community, such as Microsoft's Phi-4 and AI21's Jamba 1.6.
  • In this blog, we will describe the construction of HELMET, our key findings, and how practitioners can use HELMET to differentiate between various LCLMs in future research and applications.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Contact: hyen@cs.princeton.edu Paper: https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.02694 Website: https://princeton-nlp.github.io/HELMET Code & Data: https://github.com/princeton-nlp/HELMET.

Since we first released HELMET last October, there has been more development on long-context language models than ever before, and we are thrilled to see the adoption of HELMET by the community, such as Microsoft's Phi-4 and AI21's Jamba 1.6. After the initial release, we have added more models to our evaluation suite and conducted additional analyses. We are excited to share our new results and present HELMET at ICLR 2025!

In this blog, we will describe the construction of HELMET, our key findings, and how practitioners can use HELMET to differentiate between various LCLMs in future research and applications. Finally, we will conclude with a quickstart guide for using HELMET with HuggingFace.

In a recent development, from summarizing numerous legal documents to learning new tasks on the fly, long-context language models (LCLMs) have immense potential to change the way we use and interact with language models. Language models have been limited by their context window, which is around 2K to 8K tokens (e.g., ChatGPT, Llama-2/3). Recently, model developers have been constantly increasing the context window of their models, with recent models like GPT-4o, Claude-3, and Gemini-1.5 supporting context windows of up to millions of tokens.

However, with longer context windows, previous natural language benchmarks (e.g., Scrolls) are no longer suitable for evaluating LCLMs. Consequently, perplexity and synthetic tasks (e.g., needle-in-a-haystack) emerged as the most popular evaluation metrics for recent LCLMs, but they often do not reflect real-world performance. Model developers may also evaluate on other arbitrary datasets, which complicates model comparisons. Furthermore, existing benchmarks for LCLMs may show confusing and counterintuitive results, making it difficult to understand the strengths and weaknesses of different models (Figure 1).

In this work, we propose HELMET (How to Evaluate Long-Context Models Effectively and Thoroughly), a comprehensive benchmark for evaluating LCLMs that improves upon existing benchmarks in several ways—diversity, controllability, and reliability. We evaluate 59 recent LCLMs and find that it is crucial to evaluate models across diverse applications to understand their capabilities and frontier LCLMs are still limited on complex tasks.

With the development of LCLMs across both industry and the open-source community, it is crucial to have a reliable method for evaluating and comparing these models. However, current models are often evaluated on different benchmarks (Table 1).

In a recent development, A common practice for evaluating long-context language models is to use perplexity or synthetic tasks, such as needle-in-a-haystack (NIAH). However, recent works have shown that perplexity does not correlate well with downstream performance (Fang et al., 2024). In Figure 2, we show that synthetic tasks like NIAH do not correlate with real-world performance, but the more complex synthetic tasks achieve higher correlation with real-world tasks.

Among the existing benchmarks with realistic applications, such as ZeroScrolls (Shaman et al., 2023), LongBench (Bai et al., 2024), and InfiniteBench (Zhang et al., 2024), there are still crucial limitations:.

Thus, we propose HELMET to address these limitations and provide a comprehensive evaluation of LCLMs.

We design HELMET with the following desiderata:.

In a recent development, table 2 highlights an overview of the benchmark. In our experiments, we evaluate on input length from 8K to 128K tokens, but HELMET can be easily extended to even longer context lengths.

Industry observers note that diverse coverage: HELMET includes a diverse set of tasks, such as retrieval-augmented generation with real retrieval passages, generation with citations, and summarization. We carefully select datasets with naturally long contexts that reflect real-world applications. These datasets are complemented with reliable evaluation settings, such as model-based evaluations and human studies.

Controllable length and difficulty: An notable dimension to consider when evaluating LCLMs is the input length, as longer inputs can provide more information while challenging the model's ability to process noisy contexts. In our tasks, we can control the input length by changing the number of retrieved passages (RAG, Cite, Re-rank), the number of demonstrations (ICL), or the length of the input document (LongQA, Summ). Although LongQA and Summ cannot be easily extended to longer contexts, we intentionally chose datasets with natural documents of length far greater than 100K tokens, such that they can still be used to evaluate frontier LCLMs.

Recent findings suggest that reliable evaluation: Many existing benchmarks still use n-gram-based metrics, such as ROUGE, despite their poor correlation with human judgments (Goyal et al., 2023). We employ model-based evaluations that show better distinguishability between models and different input lengths (Figure 3). Furthermore, our human studies show that our metrics have a high agreement with human judgments.

It has been revealed that robust prompting: Existing long-context benchmarks often require models to follow instructions, but many model developments revolve around base models, which have to rely on synthetic tasks or perplexity for evaluation. Thus, we support base models for a subset of our tasks via in-context learning examples. This substantially improves the performance of base models, which is more reflective of real-world applications.

Industry observers note that our experiments and analyses include a comprehensive set of 59 LCLMs. To our knowledge, this is the most thorough and controlled comparison of long-context models on diverse applications. These models cover both leading proprietary and open-source models, and we also consider models with different architectures (e.g., full-attention transformers, hybrid architectures) and positional extrapolation techniques. In this section, we will highlight a few key findings from our experiments.

Long-context benchmarks are often constructed with specific applications in mind, such as summarization or question answering, which limits the understanding of LCLMs in a broader context. We examine model performance over a wide range of real tasks and find that different categories do not always correlate with each other (Figure 4).

While some tasks moderately correlate with each other (e.g., RAG and MS-MARCO) due to their retrieval-based nature, others show little correlation (e.g., Summ and Cite). Notably, ICL has the lowest correlation with other tasks, which suggests that it is a unique task that requires different capabilities from the model. Therefore, model developers should evaluate across these distinct axes to draw a more holistic picture of the model's capabilities.

In a recent development, we present the results of the frontier proprietary models as well as a few open-source models on HELMET. Additional results can be found in the paper and the website.

Recent findings suggest that first, we observe that open-source models lag behind closed-source models on complex tasks. Although the gap appears small on simpler tasks, such as Recall, the gap widens on more complex ones, such as Cite.

Furthermore, performance degradation with increasing lengths is category-dependent. Even the most advanced models, such as GPT-4o and Gemini, experience a significant decrease in performance on tasks like re-ranking. This change in performance cannot be observed from simply looking at the synthetic task performance.

In a recent development, finally, there is no clear winner across all categories, thereby calling for evaluation across different axes. Additional analysis, such as the performance of different positional extrapolation methods and the lost-in-the-middle phenomenon, can be found in the paper.

In a recent development, it is often expensive to run all the baselines for evaluating LCLMs, especially at long contexts given their computational and memory costs. For example, running HELMET at all lengths on a 70B model requires a node with 8 * 80GB GPUs for hundreds of GPU hours, which can be costly. By evaluating on HELMET, researchers can directly compare their models to existing ones simply by referencing our results, which cover 59 models of different sizes and architectures. You can find the leaderboard on our website.

Industry observers note that HELMET is a step towards a more comprehensive evaluation of long-context language models, but there are still many more exciting applications of LCLMs. For example, we recently released LongProc, a benchmark for evaluating LCLMs on long-form generation and following procedures, which are critical for developing reasoning models that generate tens of thousands of tokens in thinking steps. Although summarization tasks have long outputs (up to 1K tokens), LongProc focuses on even longer outputs, up to 8K tokens. Similar to HELMET, LongProc is also designed with reliable evaluation settings and diverse tasks. We are working on integrating LongProc into HELMET's evaluation suite, and we hope that this will provide a more comprehensive evaluation of LCLMs on long-form tasks.

#34900. Tiny magnetic vortices could help computers work more like your brain

Tiny magnetic vortices could help computers work more like your brain

📅 26 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (814 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Tiny magnetic structures called skyrmions could help pave the way for a newly introduced generation of computers that process information more like the human brain while using far less electricity.
  • In a recent development, A study published in the journal Nature Nanotechnology provides latest insights into how skyrmions behave and how scientists can control them.
  • Most of the research was conducted at the Institute of Physics at Johannes Gutenberg University in Mainz, Germany, with contributions from a professor at the Norwegian University of Science and Technology (NTNU).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Tiny magnetic structures called skyrmions could help pave the way for a newly introduced generation of computers that process information more like the human brain while using far less electricity. Although most people have never heard of skyrmions, these microscopic magnetic vortices may eventually play an vital role in how computers store and process data.

In a recent development, A study published in the journal Nature Nanotechnology provides latest insights into how skyrmions behave and how scientists can control them. The findings could help researchers develop smaller, more efficient computing systems and advance emerging quantum technologies.

Most of the research was conducted at the Institute of Physics at Johannes Gutenberg University in Mainz, Germany, with contributions from a professor at the Norwegian University of Science and Technology (NTNU).

"Skyrmions are small, magnetic vortices that can store information in a completely latest way," explained Asle Sudbø, who leads NTNU's Centre for Quantum Spintronics (QuSpin).

Unlike conventional technologies, which require increasing amounts of space and energy to handle growing quantities of data, skyrmions could offer a much more efficient alternative.

"Instead of the current technology, where we constantly need more space and energy to process data, skyrmions could make it possible to build much smaller and more energy-efficient data storage systems," explained Sudbø.

Tiny Magnetic Vortices Could Enable Brain-Like Computers.

The potential applications of skyrmions extend well beyond conventional data storage. They are also important to spintronics, which explores ways to use the magnetic properties of electrons in electronic devices, and to research involving topological quantum effects.

One particularly promising possibility is the development of computers that operate in ways similar to biological brains.

"These nanoscale vortices could help develop computers that resemble biological brains," stated Sudbø.

Industry observers note that rather than relying on conventional transistor-based computing, such systems could use magnetism to process information. In principle, this approach could dramatically reduce electricity consumption, potentially allowing future computers to perform complex tasks with very little energy.

Turning that possibility into practical technology, however, requires scientists to understand exactly how skyrmions behave and how to manipulate them reliably.

The latest research represents an crucial advance toward that goal.

Scientists Film Magnetic Skyrmion Lattices Melting for the First Time.

Skyrmions do not always exist as isolated magnetic structures. Under certain conditions, they organize themselves into repeating patterns known as lattices, resembling the orderly arrangement of atoms in a crystal, but on a much smaller scale.

Scientists can manipulate these arrangements, a capability that could be essential for using skyrmions in future computing devices.

In the upcoming study, researchers achieved something that had not been demonstrated before. They recorded the melting of a magnetic skyrmion lattice as it happened while simultaneously controlling individual skyrmions.

Industry observers note that "For the first time, researchers have managed to film how a magnetic skyrmion lattice melts in real time, while simultaneously being able to manipulate each individual skyrmion directly as they film it. For example, both their shape and size can be changed 'on the fly'," remarked Sudbø.

Recent findings suggest that the ability to observe this process directly provides a clearer picture of how skyrmions respond when their organized structures break apart. It also allows researchers to study how changing the size and shape of individual magnetic vortices affects their behavior.

A New Step Toward Energy-Efficient Computing.

Understanding how skyrmions behave during the breakdown of their lattices could help scientists develop more precise ways to control them. That control is particularly key if these magnetic structures are to become useful components in future computer systems.

The findings therefore offer more than a new way to observe an unusual magnetic phenomenon. They provide information that could help researchers overcome challenges involved in developing practical skyrmion-based technologies.

Recent findings suggest that "The findings give us latest insight into how these types of particles behave. This could therefore become important for the development of more energy-efficient computer technology in the future," mentioned Sudbø.

Although substantial development is still needed before skyrmions can be used in everyday computing devices, the research highlights their potential for improving data storage, enabling new computing architectures, and supporting advances in quantum technology.

By learning to observe and manipulate these tiny magnetic vortices in real time, scientists are gaining capabilities that could eventually help reshape the design of computers.

"This could revolutionize the way we think about computers," concluded Sudbø.

This guide compares six options, explains how each works and points out where each one falls short. Plans and limits change often, so confirm current details on each vendor's site.

Caption extraction. The tool pulls the captions attached to a video, either written by the creator or generated automatically by YouTube. It is fast and usually free, but it is only as good as those captions. It has been revealed that fresh speech recognition. The tool takes the audio and runs its own speech-to-text model. This can be more accurate on difficult recordings and works when no captions exist, but it takes longer and often costs money.

Lynote is built for exactly this job. Paste a YouTube link, search by keyword or add a playlist, and it returns a timestamped transcript with an AI summary. Batch mode accepts up to 10 videos at once. The tool lists transcription in more than 100 languages, translation into 25, auto-chapters, one-click copy and TXT download, with SRT export also mentioned. The page says transcripts are free, with no sign-up required.

Best for: Students, researchers and marketers who want a quick, readable transcript or summary from a public video without installing anything.

Limitations: It extracts YouTube captions, so videos without captions cannot be processed. If the original captions are poor, the transcript will be too. For critical accuracy, review the text or use a service with human verification.

Best for: Quick lookups on videos that already have decent captions.

Notta transcribes uploaded audio and video files and also accepts YouTube links. It lists support for 58 languages, real-time and bilingual transcription, and AI Notes that produce summaries and action items. A free plan includes 120 transcription minutes per month at the time of writing.
