The hidden human intelligence of design

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2057 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fastcompany

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Here’s a scenario you can likely relate to in our age of automated systems: Someone underestimates what you do to deliver a product or service.
  • According to recent reports, here’s a scenario you can likely relate to in our age of automated systems: Someone underestimates what you do to deliver a product or service.
  • Often overlooked are the years of education and experience that shape what you do, along with the complex decisions you make with judgment, empathy, wisdom, and humility.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Here’s a scenario you can likely relate to in our age of automated systems: Someone underestimates what you do to deliver a product or service. They are solely focused on the result and say, “I could do that with AI.” Often overlooked are the years of education and experience that shape what you do, along with the complex decisions you make with judgment, empathy, wisdom, and humility. We are increasingly seeing this in the architectural industry. And it’s more than just a feeling or a hunch. Recently, the U.S. Department of Education moved to alter the definition of professional degrees to exclude architecture. This demonstrates a serious misunderstanding of what architecture entails. The creative professionals delivering complex projects in the built environment are experts: systems thinkers choreographing designs that shape environments, cultures, and communities. DESIGN AND EMOTION Design decisions are interconnected, but that complexity is often underestimated. Changes made after work is underway can require significant rework and additional layers of coordination, impacting budget and schedule. Even seemingly small change requests can ripple through other systems and affect project value. Behind every built environment is a constellation of decisions and balancing acts that are invisible to the end user. A successful design blends noiselessly into daily life. When everything is working, and spaces are intuitive, comfortable, and almost anticipatory in supporting your needs, you rarely think about the creativity, imagination, and coordination behind each design and engineering decision. Architecture’s value is its ability to make us feel something as we enter a space before we even understand why we are experiencing those emotions. The reverence of a cathedral, the excitement of a stadium, the safety and security of a home—those emotional and physical reactions do not happen by chance. Each response is a specific result of a team’s design decisions. IMPACT VERSUS HOURS There’s an idea that generative AI can replace nearly any profession. This is a tough pill to swallow for those who’ve spent years or decades honing their craft. But this way of thinking raises a deeper question: Is worth measured by the visible impact you create or the hours you log? I know architects aren’t the only ones who experience this. Leaders in finance, medicine, tech, and other fields hear from people who see the tip of the iceberg and don’t realize how much is below the surface. When they don’t understand the extent of expertise, they don’t value it. They think it can be done quickly and simply. The final output is neat and clean. But the reality is that the design process is often complex. It involves researching, discussing, debating, ideating, innovating, finding common ground, and making decisions. One skill an architect learns over time is listening beyond the client’s initial brief, identifying added value to the design program. Early in your career, you treat a brief as a rulebook. Over time, you learn how to advocate for a vision often shaped by a process of listening, challenging, and refining. It’s important for us to embrace productive friction, in life and in this discipline. It’s the moments that must be experienced, including moments of friction when we are challenged and must overcome some adversity, that are more formative and leave a lasting impact. 6 DESIGN AREAS REQUIRING HUMAN SKILLS Consider these six challenging parts of any design process that require human expertise: 1. Consensus building: While AI can pull data from multiple sources, it cannot negotiate and compromise with diverse stakeholders. People disagree. An architect is a bridge between clients, project partners, and city officials. Architects have to balance vision with constraints, and to resolve disagreements and conflicts among all parties. 2. Constructability and feasibility: It’s impressive when AI can generate a beautiful rendering in seconds. But what if the rendering isn’t practical or realistic? Architects must make the design come alive in the real world. They need to know, through knowledge and experience, how a design will perform when built, and to exercise judgment based on wisdom. 3. Intelligence beyond pattern recognition: Despite the word “intelligence,” does AI think? Or does it recognize patterns, relying on existing data to predict future outcomes? As today’s problems grow increasingly complex, the synthesis of this complex data to anticipate outcomes is a powerful tool. Where AI recognizes patterns, architects bring discernment, interpreting data through a lens that is contextual and time-sensitive, creating solutions tailored to the histories and needs of specific sites and the communities that use them. 4. Risk management and resilience: Architects are tasked with thinking about future stressors on a building. Based on historic precedent, they consider what long-term resilience is required of buildings they are designing. AI can’t assume that human element of taking responsibility and accountability. IBM’s training manual in 1979 stated, “A computer can never be held accountable; therefore, a computer must never make a management decision.” AI doesn’t understand that lives will be seriously affected if its design isn’t resilient; it’s imperative to leverage the tool responsibly. 5. Challenge assumptions as a trusted advisor: We want to assume the best of those we work with, but trust isn’t easy to build. It’s built through real-world troubleshooting and problem-solving. Sometimes that means saying no. Anyone who ever had a chatbot agree with everything they remarked understands that AI often tells you what you want to hear. 6. Center work around human experience and emotion: Joy Evans Therapeutic Recreation Center in Washington, D.C.—the only public recreation center in the region offering therapeutic recreational programming—exemplifies the importance of designing for a range of human experiences. To make the center a welcoming and inclusive place for people of all ages and abilities, our designers needed a thorough human understanding of what made people feel safe, seen, and inspired. AI can grasp key tenets of accessibility and belonging abstractly, but doesn’t understand human vulnerability. When we recognize and respect these messy parts of the process, we understand that human professionals can’t be replaced. It’s important we help our clients and customers understand this too, demonstrating how we can use the best of AI while emphasizing the value of human judgment and perspective. Steven McKay is CEO of DLR Group.

Improving Hugging Face Model Access for Kaggle Users

📅 14 May 2025 | ⏱️ 3 min read (535 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Kaggle and Hugging Face users are part of one AI community.
  • Beginning today, Kaggle is launching an integration that enhances visibility and discoverability for Hugging Face models directly on Kaggle.
  • You can navigate from Hugging Face models to Kaggle and vice versa.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Kaggle and Hugging Face users are part of one AI community. That’s why we’re excited to announce our plans to bring our platforms and communities closer to better serve AI developers everywhere.

Beginning today, Kaggle is launching an integration that enhances visibility and discoverability for Hugging Face models directly on Kaggle.

You can navigate from Hugging Face models to Kaggle and vice versa. Start by visiting a Hugging Face model page like Qwen/Qwen3-1.7B. To use it in a Kaggle Notebook, you can click on “Use this model” and select “Kaggle” to open up a Kaggle notebook with a pre-populated code snippet to load the model. You can do the same from a Hugging Face model page on Kaggle by clicking the “Code” button.

When you run a notebook on Kaggle that references a model hosted on Hugging Face Hub, we will automatically generate a Hugging Face model page if one doesn’t exist already. You don’t need to make any special changes to your code. Additionally, when you make your notebook public, it will automatically show on the “Code” tab of the Kaggle model page.

Industry observers note that discover Hugging Face models and explore all the community examples in public notebooks in one place on Kaggle at https://www.kaggle.com/models. As more Hugging Face models are used on Kaggle, the number of models and associated code examples you can explore for inspiration will grow.

According to recent reports, when browsing Hugging Face models on Kaggle, we want to make it easy for you to navigate back to Hugging Face to explore additional details, metadata, community usage in Hugging Face Spaces, discussion, and more. Simply click “Open in Hugging Face” on the Kaggle model page.

In a recent development, if you use a private Hugging Face model in your Kaggle notebook, authenticate via your Hugging Face account as normal (add your HF_TOKEN in the “Add-ons > Secrets” menu in the notebook editor). A Hugging Face model page won’t be generated on Kaggle.

If you want to access a consent-gated model in your Kaggle notebook, you’ll need to request access to it using a Hugging Face account and follow the prompts on your browser's Hugging Face model page as normal. Hugging Face has documentation to guide you through this process. Otherwise, the integration will work the same as for non-gated models.

We’re actively working on a solution to seamlessly use Hugging Face models in Kaggle competitions that require offline notebook submissions. While this will take a few more months to complete, we believe the wait will be worth it.

Sources indicate that you can read Kaggle’s position on “AI Competitions as the gold standard for empirical rigor for GenAI evaluation” to understand why it’s so key for us to get this part of the integration right! But tl;dr – Kaggle is highly sensitive to data leakage and its impact on model contamination. Our goal is to design this integration to preserve the integrity of our competitions and their vital role in the industry, while enabling seamless access for Kaggle competitors to build with the best models from Hugging Face!

We’d love to hear your feedback in the meantime - share your thoughts and ideas here!

Why ‘you don’t have to use AI’ is the newly introduced AI pitch

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 15 min read (3019 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fastcompany

⏱️ ~15 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Watching Adobe’s keynote presentation at the 24th annual Max conference in Miami this week, I couldn’t help but think about the tightrope the software giant is walking with AI, and how similar it is to what the media industry is going through.
  • Watching Adobe’s keynote presentation at the 24th annual Max conference in Miami this week, I couldn’t help but think about the tightrope the software giant is walking with AI, and how similar it is to what the media industry is going through.
  • According to recent reports, at Adobe’s last two annual Max events, AI was a huge emphasis.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Watching Adobe’s keynote presentation at the 24th annual Max conference in Miami this week, I couldn’t help but think about the tightrope the software giant is walking with AI, and how similar it is to what the media industry is going through. In both cases, there’s a desire to be AI-forward and skate to where the puck is going. At the same time, they need to deal with a hostile crowd—meaning the growing backlash against AI among many of their customers. At Adobe’s last two annual Max events, AI was a huge emphasis. The company touted AI features, including ways to generate content directly in its Creative Cloud apps, such as Photoshop and Premiere. Adobe hyped up Firefly, which was then mostly associated with the company’s image models. In 2024, Adobe told the audience that “2024 will go down as the year that creativity changed forever.” In 2025, the headliners were a latest Firefly image model and a lineup of third-party models from Google, OpenAI, Runway, and others, and “choice” mostly meant choosing which AI model to use. The lone nod to skeptics was a passing aside: “Of course, you can ignore it all as well.” This year, the tone shifted. In fact, one of the first things incoming CEO Anil Chakravarthy emphasized during the opening keynote was that people didn’t have to use AI if they didn’t want to. “Some of you don’t want to have anything to do with AI,” he mentioned, promising to give those users “the precision and control that you’re looking for, and the option to not use AI.” Instead of a new Firefly model number, the keynote spotlighted upgrades with no AI in them at all, like a rebuilt color mode in Premiere and Dynamic Text in Illustrator. Firefly is still an area of focus, but it’s evolved into a catch-all creative studio, more like Figma than an AI model. (Disclosure: Adobe paid for my travel to the Max conference, though it had no input on this column.) AI-optional doesn’t mean AI-free None of this is to say Adobe is walking away from AI. Far from it: During that same keynote, Chakravarthy announced Adobe would be providing a way for AI services to access Creative Cloud applications directly through the model context protocol (MCP) standard. That means AI users will be able to have Claude, ChatGPT, or Gemini act as an agent, effectively “driving” Photoshop and other Creative Cloud apps to edit projects, create content, and export files directly on their computers. The integrations go into private beta testing in early 2027. Adobe already provides an AI connector that works similarly, but the MCPs would take things to a new level of precision and control. Jesus Diaz has a great breakdown of exactly how they would work and what it means for creators. In addition, Adobe is building out its own agents. The new Creative Agent is essentially an Adobe chatbot: You describe what you want, and the agent handles the execution in the appropriate app. It’s now in beta inside Premiere, Illustrator, InDesign, After Effects, and Frame.io. All this makes it clear Adobe isn’t slowing down on AI. It has, however, recognized that a great bifurcation is taking place, one that’s affecting all industries to some extent, but especially the media. On the one hand, you have your AI skeptics, the customers who are suspicious of AI generally and AI-generated or -assisted content specifically. And on the other, you have the AI enthusiasts, the ones who are using AI to enhance and speed up their work, including through tools from other companies. This is the AI tightrope, and all businesses will need to navigate it over the next few years. Not just because AI represents “the future” in some vague sense, but because, if it does, it opens up a new kind of customer. Now everyone knows kung fu My business is actually a pretty good example of this. I use various software, including Photoshop and Premiere, to help produce content like The Media Copilot podcast. But I’m not a creator per se, and I’m probably using only about 10% of the features that would help my use case. For many, that skill gap is the difference between subscribing and not. But an agent that bridges the gap could mean Adobe customers are no longer just enthusiasts and experts. Suddenly, we’re all Neo in the Matrix: Just plug an agent into your workstream, and you know kung fu. In fact, one of the Max keynote demos was more or less my exact workflow: an outside AI agent turning a long-form podcast into a batch of short clips for social media. There’s also an urgency here, and again, my use case is a good example. I’ve already begun off-loading some of my production process to agents. Claude Code and OpenAI Codex are both excellent at analyzing workflows and recommending software solutions that they (not I) can operate. Often, it’s open-source software that gets the job done at virtually no cost other than the tokens I expend. And Adobe users can even employ computer use—in which the AI uses your machine, just as you would—to operate the software. It’s messier than an MCP, but it gets the job done, and AI is getting better at this by the day. In other words, the AI world is moving toward agentic work, with or without Adobe. Businesses of all kinds are beginning to demand this kind of functionality, and even if open-source software is cheaper, there are advantages to using commercial software. Security, reliability, and auditability are all very crucial to enterprises. And it’s mutually beneficial to Adobe, since the number of licenses those businesses buy will no longer be limited by the number of experts they have. Notably, the MCP integrations require the apps to be installed and licensed on the user’s machine. Even when an agent is the one driving Photoshop, someone is still paying for the seat. Media’s version of the same customer There’s a corollary here in media. As people turn more and more to AI answers for information, it means bots scrape all kinds of sites to find the best possible answer. A consequence of this is that niche sites—in particular B2B media—have become some of the most sought-after sources on the web. TollBit’s latest “State of the Bots” report ranks B2B and professional sites among the most heavily scraped categories it tracks, with scraping up 62% from Q2 2025 to Q4 2025. Their specialized knowledge might sometimes be impenetrable to mainstream audiences, but never to AI agents. They can rapidly parse the bits that are important and relevant, then break them down in a way that’s understandable to anyone. Just like with those Photoshop agents, lack of expertise is no longer a barrier to adoption. But what about those AI skeptics? They’re an important part of any company’s existing customer base, and they’ve made their views clear: They don’t want to see AI in the content they consume. I’ve written about the problem with AI tells in text, and the same goes for images and video: Audiences consistently say they don’t like them. That doesn’t mean all AI is bad, and many Adobe AI-powered features garnered lots of applause at Max. But it needs to be in the right context. A good rule of thumb: AI behind the scenes is generally okay, but you need to be careful with generative content. The audience research lines up almost exactly. In the Reuters Institute’s “Generative AI and News Report 2025,” only 12% of people said they were comfortable with news generated entirely by AI, compared with 62% for news produced entirely by humans. But 55% were fine with AI fixing spelling and grammar. Most media companies have arrived at a similar place. There are tantalizing opportunities for content to reach new audiences through AI search engines and agent protocols like MCP. At the same time, they need to tread lightly when implementing artificial intelligence in their own operations, lest they lose trust with their existing audience. That’s the AI tightrope, and staying balanced is obviously the trick to moving forward. Getting the agents to pay up But what’s on the other end? At least for Adobe, the answer is clearer: a new and potentially huge customer base that doesn’t want to use tools but is happy for agents to. For media, the other end of the rope is murkier. The agents are already here, reading trade publications and national news alike, but most of them are still taking what they find without paying for it. AI apps send publishers a sliver of the traffic Google does, and the deals that would make up the difference are stuck in courtrooms and licensing negotiations. Adobe found a way to charge for the agents using its tools. Until the media figures out how to get agents to pay for the privilege of reading content, it’s walking the same tightrope, just without a net.

It’s messier than an MCP, but it gets the job done, and AI is getting better at this by the day.

In a recent development, in other words, the AI world is moving toward agentic work, with or without Adobe. Businesses of all kinds are beginning to demand this kind of functionality, and even if open-source software is cheaper, there are advantages to using commercial software. Security, reliability, and auditability are all very important to enterprises. And it’s mutually beneficial to Adobe, since the number of licenses those businesses buy will no longer be limited by the number of experts they have. Notably, the MCP integrations require the apps to be installed and licensed on the user’s machine. Even when an agent is the one driving Photoshop, someone is still paying for the seat.

There’s a corollary here in media. As people turn more and more to AI answers for information, it means bots scrape all kinds of sites to find the best possible answer. A consequence of this is that niche sites—in particular B2B media—have become some of the most sought-after sources on the web. TollBit’s latest “State of the Bots” report ranks B2B and professional sites among the most heavily scraped categories it tracks, with scraping up 62% from Q2 2025 to Q4 2025.

Their specialized knowledge might sometimes be impenetrable to mainstream audiences, but never to AI agents. They can quickly parse the bits that are vital and relevant, then break them down in a way that’s understandable to anyone. Just like with those Photoshop agents, lack of expertise is no longer a barrier to adoption.

It has been revealed that but what about those AI skeptics? They’re an important part of any company’s existing customer base, and they’ve made their views clear: They don’t want to see AI in the content they consume. I’ve written about the problem with AI tells in text, and the same goes for images and video: Audiences consistently say they don’t like them. That doesn’t mean all AI is bad, and many Adobe AI-powered features garnered lots of applause at Max. But it needs to be in the right context.

A good rule of thumb: AI behind the scenes is generally okay, but you need to be careful with generative content. The audience research lines up almost exactly. In the Reuters Institute’s “Generative AI and News Report 2025,” only 12% of people said they were comfortable with news generated entirely by AI, compared with 62% for news produced entirely by humans. But 55% were fine with AI fixing spelling and grammar.

It has been revealed that most media companies have arrived at a similar place. There are tantalizing opportunities for content to reach latest audiences through AI search engines and agent protocols like MCP. At the same time, they need to tread lightly when implementing artificial intelligence in their own operations, lest they lose trust with their existing audience. That’s the AI tightrope, and staying balanced is obviously the trick to moving forward.

But what’s on the other end? At least for Adobe, the answer is clearer: a new and potentially huge customer base that doesn’t want to use tools but is happy for agents to. For media, the other end of the rope is murkier. The agents are already here, reading trade publications and national news alike, but most of them are still taking what they find without paying for it. AI apps send publishers a sliver of the traffic Google does, and the deals that would make up the difference are stuck in courtrooms and licensing negotiations.

Adobe found a way to charge for the agents using its tools. Until the media figures out how to get agents to pay for the privilege of reading content, it’s walking the same tightrope, just without a net.

RTO means women risk doing the office housework all over again

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1177 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fastcompany

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that women have already been disproportionately affected by return-to-office mandates, being expected to juggle work, childcare, household responsibilities, and doing the mental gymnastics to stay on top of it all.
  • Women have already been disproportionately affected by return-to-office mandates, being expected to juggle work, childcare, household responsibilities, and doing the mental gymnastics to stay on top of it all.
  • Usually, the conversation about mental load centers on household chores, such as who is responsible for doing the laundry, planning meals, and buying the groceries.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that women have already been disproportionately affected by return-to-office mandates, being expected to juggle work, childcare, household responsibilities, and doing the mental gymnastics to stay on top of it all. Now, old-fashioned assumptions about the unpaid work women are expected to take on in the office risk adding to that burden. Usually, the conversation about mental load centers on household chores, such as who is responsible for doing the laundry, planning meals, and buying the groceries. And it’s women who are more likely to do more domestic labor even when both partners are employed full time. One 2024 study of 3,000 US parents found that mothers took primary responsibility for 71% of household tasks requiring mental effort, compared with 45% for fathers. It happens at work, too, where it’s known as “office housework.” These are the unpaid, often unrecognized tasks that keep an organization running but rarely help the people doing them advance their careers. Women therefore can end up doing more work without getting any credit for it. And RTO might be making things worse. A study of 1,091 professional women in the US found that 31% reported experiencing everyday gender discrimination when working on-site, compared with 17% when working remotely. This included performing tasks that weren’t their responsibility. The results suggest that being physically present can expose women to more everyday gender discrimination and create more opportunities for these assumptions to surface. The problem is also evident in the UK. In a new survey of 2,000 working women and men by advocacy group Co-operatives UK, 22% of women noted they’d been asked to do paperwork outside their role, 21% had been asked to clean or tidy the office, and 20% had been asked to make coffee for senior leaders. Overall, nearly half (49%) of women said they’d been asked more than once to do something outside their role, such as making tea or booking a meeting room. Women have been highlighting the problem on social media, sharing their experiences and how they push back against the assumption that they’ll take on these tasks. One content creator, Alex Schudy, said she had noticed colleagues using what she described as “weaponized incompetence” to try to get her to take notes in meetings, often by throwing her a compliment to disguise it. In her video on TikTok, she said she let the “silence linger” when one colleague suggested she do it because her handwriting was neat and she was “organized.” She politely declined, explaining that she needed to focus on presenting her part of the meeting. Someone else was designated the notetaker instead. Another creator, Anna Kennedy, described in a video how much office housework she had come to realise women were doing — from keeping track of action items and chasing colleagues to making sure feedback was acted upon. “Things that keep the machine moving fundamentally, but are not rewarded or seen in a performance review,” she said. “I’m never, I swear to God, never seeing men doing this kind of work.” As more employees settle back into office life, many hope there have been changes for the better, particularly around work-life balance and flexibility. But some of the oldest workplace habits seem stubbornly resistant to change, and it’s time women stopped being expected to pick up the slack. Ultimately, they shouldn’t have to spend their working days doing the jobs that keep everyone else organized, only to be left behind as everyone else speeds ahead.

The Transformers Library: standardizing model definitions

📅 15 May 2025 | ⏱️ 5 min read (922 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • TLDR: Going forward, we're aiming for Transformers to be the pivot across frameworks: if a model architecture is supported by transformers, you can expect it to be supported in the rest of the ecosystem.
  • In a recent development, transformers was created in 2019, shortly following the release of the BERT Transformer model.
  • Transformers now supports 300+ model architectures, with an average of ~3 new architectures added every week.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

TLDR: Going forward, we're aiming for Transformers to be the pivot across frameworks: if a model architecture is supported by transformers, you can expect it to be supported in the rest of the ecosystem.

In a recent development, transformers was created in 2019, shortly following the release of the BERT Transformer model. Since then, we've continuously aimed to add state-of-the-art architectures, initially focused on NLP, then growing to Audio and computer vision. Today, transformers is the default library for LLMs and VLMs in the Python ecosystem.

Transformers now supports 300+ model architectures, with an average of ~3 new architectures added every week. We have aimed for these architectures to be released in a timely manner; having day-0 support for the most sought-after architectures (Llamas, Qwens, GLMs, etc.).

Over time, Transformers has become a central component in the ML ecosystem, becoming one of the most complete toolkits in terms of model diversity; it's integrated in all popular training frameworks such as Axolotl, Unsloth, DeepSpeed, FSDP, PyTorch-Lightning, TRL, Nanotron, etc.

Recently, we've been working hand in hand with the most popular inference engines (vLLM, SGLang, TGI, ...) for them to use transformers as a backend. The value added is significant: as soon as a model is added to transformers, it becomes available in these inference engines, while taking advantage of the strengths each engine provides: inference optimizations, specialized kernels, dynamic batching, etc.

As an example, here is how you would work with the transformers backend in vLLM:.

That's all it takes for a new model to enjoy super-fast and production-grade serving with vLLM!

Read more about it in the vLLM documentation.

It has been revealed that we've also been working very closely with llama.cpp and MLX so that the implementations between transformers and these modeling libraries have great interoperability. For example, thanks to a significant community effort, it's now very easy to load GGUF files in transformers for further fine-tuning. Conversely, transformers models can be easily converted to GGUF files for use with llama.cpp.

The same is true for MLX, where the transformers' safetensors files are directly compatible with MLX's models.

We are super proud that the transformers format is being adopted by the community, bringing a lot of interoperability we all benefit from. Train a model with Unsloth, deploy it with SGLang, and export it to llama.cpp to run locally! We aim to keep supporting the community going forward.

Recent findings suggest that to make it easier for the community to use transformers as a reference for model definitions, we strive to significantly reduce the barrier to model contributions. We have been doing this effort for a few years, but we'll accelerate significantly over the next few weeks:.

As a model user, in the future you should see even more interoperability in the tools that you use.

This does not mean that we intend to lock you in using transformers in your experiments; rather, it means that thanks to this modeling standardization, you can expect the tools that you use for training, for inference, and for production, to efficiently work together.

As a model creator, this means that a single contribution will get your model available in all downstream libraries that have integrated that modeling implementation. We have seen this many times over the years: releasing a model is stressful and integrating in all crucial libraries is often a significant time-sink.

By standardizing the model implementation in a community-driven manner, we hope to lower the barrier of contributions to the field across libraries.

Recent findings suggest that we firmly believe this renewed direction will help standardize an ecosystem which is often at risk of fragmentation. We'd love to hear your feedback on the direction the team has decided to take; and of changes we could do to get there. Please come and see us over at the transformers-community support tab on the Hub!

Industry observers note that awesome news! Transformers being the default access point for as many models on day 0 as well as in being able to use the inference engine of choice is an epic goal!

if a model architecture is supported by transformers, you can expect it to be supported in the rest of the ecosystem.

It's interesting, but it seems regardless of the TLDR, Llama.CPP maintains its own implementation and so won't benefit from any "day-0 support" for latest architectures in Transfomers. I was kind of hoping Llama would get straight Transformer compatibility for a moment.

It's not clear what, if anything, is changing there.

You're entirely correct that llama.cpp maintains its own implementation; we've been working hand-in-hand with the team to get better intercompatibility however: export between frameworks on both sides (from transformers to llama.cpp, and vice-versa).

Additionally, with the frequent VLM releases happening recently, we've been working directly with @ngxson to have the implementations day-0 (or week-0) in llama.cpp when the implementation already exists in transformers.

We won't have "automatic day-0 support" as the two libs have different backends; but we can still try by making the two more compatible, reducing the time needed to get there.

In a recent development, thanks @lysandre . Apologies if I sounded overly negative at all, it's a very good goal.

According to recent reports, since I doubt Llama.cpp would implement Transformers directly as VLM did (although that would be nice), perhaps an in-between project is possible using the low-level C bindings Llama provides. I believe that's how llama-cpp-python and similar work.

Then again I'm not sure how much benefit there is, but food for thought.

The future of live entertainment

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1955 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fastcompany

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Digital saturation is reshaping nearly every dimension of our lives in this age of artificiality, transforming how we work, communicate, and experience the world around us.
  • Industry observers note that change is in the air.
  • Amid this profound transformation, our desire for experiences that are deeply human has never been greater.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Change is in the air. Digital saturation is reshaping nearly every dimension of our lives in this age of artificiality, transforming how we work, communicate, and experience the world around us. Amid this profound transformation, our desire for experiences that are deeply human has never been greater. Technology can do so much, including simulating interaction and placing nearly limitless entertainment at our fingertips. But it cannot fully replicate formative live entertainment moments like the collective anticipation before a performance or the emotional release of thousands of people experiencing the same unforgettable moment together. Human beings are fundamentally social. We are drawn to one another and transformed by shared experience. Gathering is part of who we are. That fundamental human desire places us on the precipice of a cultural renaissance. Throughout history, moments of mass disruption have repeatedly created the conditions for extraordinary periods of advancement in art, science, architecture, technology, and design. These moments force societies to question familiar assumptions and search for upcoming ways to understand one another. We are entering such a moment now. In this emerging age of artificiality, human creativity will command a new premium. So will presence. The experiences we cannot download, automate, or predict will become more valuable precisely because they are real. For designers (and any type of creative), this is an extraordinary opportunity. We have the ability—and responsibility—to shape the experiences that define the next era of culture. 4 IDEAS TO GUIDE THE NEXT ERA OF CULTURE History demonstrates that people are remarkably resilient. When confronted with uncertainty or moments of radical change, we search for reasons to believe in what comes next, then adapt accordingly. What follows are four ideas that can help ensure this latest cultural renaissance is a period of meaningful transformation that unites people globally for a shared purpose: connection. 1. The importance of optimism  That instinct remains powerful today. According to recent research from VML Intelligence, 69% of respondents regularly feel hopeful about the future. Beneath the anxiety surrounding technological and cultural change, optimism persists. That optimism matters because hope rarely remains an individual emotion. People seek opportunities to express it collectively. Live entertainment gives physical form to that desire. Watching Lionel Messi with his foot on the ball in the 90th minute of the FIFA World Cup, a stadium erupting in victory, a concert audience singing a chorus with Taylor Swift, or a theater falling completely silent at the same emotional moment reveals something profound. Emotion becomes amplified when it’s shared. The most successful venues build anticipation and entice participation. They create the conditions for strangers to feel connected. As optimism becomes a defining force in the next cultural era, the places that bring people together will become increasingly important expressions of collective possibility. 2. The return of real The renewed interest in analog experiences is already visible across culture. Vinyl records, tapes, and physical media have returned to prominence. Film cameras and Polaroids are reappearing at concerts and celebrations. Tactile pursuits such as journaling and knitting are attracting new generations. These behaviors are sometimes dismissed as nostalgia. But they represent something more consequential: a desire for agency and authenticity. It is a tangible connection in a world of infinite, algorithmically delivered content. People want experiences they can touch and remember. They want the imperfect and the unpredictable. They desire the unrepeatable. Live entertainment is the ultimate expression of that desire. No two performances are the same. No crowd produces the same energy. No professional athlete reacts in the same way in that critical winning moment. The possibility that something unexpected might happen is the source of its power. Designers are beginning to respond through spaces that encourage deeper presence and participation. Listening rooms, intimate performance spaces, flexible venues, and carefully choreographed social environments are creating new ways to experience music and culture together. In the age of artificiality, the real becomes rare. Rarity creates the ultimate value. 3. From experience to transformation This cultural recalibration aligns with B. Joseph Pine’s concept of the transformation economy. This is the idea that people increasingly seek experiences that change them. Businesses and institutions will increasingly be judged by what they provide and by whether the experiences they create feel meaningful and transformative. This is especially true in sports and live entertainment, where identity, ritual, and emotion are inseparable from the event itself. The 2026 FIFA World Cup offered a powerful expression of this idea. Supporters traveled from across the globe not simply to watch soccer, but to participate in one of humanity’s great, shared traditions. The matches mattered, but so did the pilgrimage, the gathering, the rituals, and the sense of belonging to a global community. The same principle exists at every scale, spanning the intimacy of a listening room to the collective roar of a stadium and everything in between. Each can become a place where human connection is forged, moments that become treasured memories. 4. A collective opportunity awaits The next era of live entertainment will be defined by how thoughtfully technology is used to deepen, not displace, the human experience. Our greatest opportunity is to design places that encourage people to look up from their devices, toward the performance and toward one another. Places that transform attendance into participation, audiences into communities, and fleeting moments into enduring memories. These places give physical form to the things artificial intelligence cannot manufacture; chief among them, authentic, spontaneous, and shared emotion. The conditions for a cultural renaissance are already here. Its character, however, is not predetermined. It will be shaped by the choices of many, including cultural and entertainment leaders. Let’s collectively embrace an opportunity to design and lead a new era. It’s one that doesn’t come often and can spark lasting impacts that will positively influence generations to come. Brian Mirakian is senior principal at Populous.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Weekly. Free. One click to leave.

7 Day Free Trial. Cancel Anytime.

Industry observers note that A device disconnects halfway through a test. The application reports a timeout, the firmware restarts, and the next attempt succeeds. Where should you start?

For developers working with connected devices, browser interfaces, or hardware prototypes, an application error is often only the final symptom. Replacing code without recording the conditions around a failure can leave you chasing the wrong layer.

It has been revealed that this tutorial builds a small browser-based diagnostic log. It records measurements, preserves the test conditions, and exports evidence for another developer to review. You need basic HTML and JavaScript knowledge; no framework or connected instrument is required.

1. Define the question before collecting data Consider a hypothetical development board that disconnects when a peripheral starts. Several explanations remain possible: a firmware exception, a transport problem, or a power supply issue. Start with a testable question: “Does the measured supply voltage change when this peripheral starts?” That question tells you what to record and what to keep constant.

Sources indicate that use a known-good board of the same revision where available. Match the firmware, cable, supply, peripheral, and workload. A comparison loses value when several conditions change together.

Record the observation separately from the explanation:.

Industry observers note that the hypothesis remains provisional. A reading taken after the device restarts does not establish what happened during the failure.

2. Choose evidence that answers the question Application logs, firmware traces, and bench measurements answer different questions. A timeout establishes that an operation did not finish in time; it does not identify a failed component.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Since the days of MySpace’s Top 8, social media has made it easy to hurt your friends’ feelings. Some platforms make it easy to judge relative friendship, like Snapchat’s publicly viewable “Best Friends” feature. Instagram, however, keeps people’ social dynamics under wraps from one another, with accounts unable to see when someone unfollows them. Instagram head Adam Mosseri has previously stated the platform hasn’t introduced a “who unfollowed me” feature so that users feel free to unfollow whomever they please without fear of judgment or tension. But a new tool from Instagram’s parent manufacturer Meta is shaking things up. Its AI assistant Muse has an apparently petty personality under its cute and cuddly exterior—and it’s happy to help users spot who isn’t following them back and then unfollow them en masse. How Muse can purge your Instagram Social media users have discovered that Muse can sort through the people they follow on Instagram and point out any non-mutual connections. Though third-party apps have offered similar features in the past, they’re notorious for getting accounts flagged and taken down from Instagram. Muse, as an in-house app, doesn’t pose the same risk. One Instagram user who tried out the feature, Khalil Roberts, told Wired about his experience using Muse. Roberts gave Muse the prompt, “Can you show me a list of people (non celebrity) that [don’t] follow me back on Instagram, and can you unfollow them for me.” It swiftly returned an Excel spreadsheet with 151 accounts that fit his criteria, then asked if he wanted to follow through on unfollowing them. Roberts was among the chorus on social media singing Muse’s praises for letting them purge such accounts so easily. “I just cleared 80+ chopped hos who thought I was a fan,” one user posted. “Just unfollowed 1000+ people on IG,” another user boasted, crediting Muse in a follow-up post. Meta’s secret menu Though Muse’s potential for pettiness is a much-requested feature, it’s only being spread through word of mouth. Meta itself isn’t advertising the capability—or at least not anymore. In October, Los Angeles-based social media consultant Rachel Karten noticed a Meta ad on Instagram touting that Muse could let users “see who unfollowed you each week.” “I get that this is technically a requested feature but wouldn’t it lead to more resentment towards your own platform?” Karten asked in a post sharing a screenshot of the ad. i get that this is technically a requested feature but wouldn’t it lead to more resentment towards your own platform? pic.twitter.com/SbM6VdcdhV— Rachel Karten (@milkkarten) October 24, 2026 Indeed, Instagram has since taken down the ad, as a Meta representative confirmed to Business Insider. Still, the feature remains active in Muse—as long as users know to ask for it.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In this blogpost, we present the key highlights and rationales about the Falcon-Edge series - a collection of powerful, universal, and fine-tunable language models available in ternary format, based on the BitNet architecture.
  • Drawing from our experience with BitNet, Falcon-Edge introduces and validates an newly introduced pre-training paradigm that delivers a full-scope output from a single training process, simultaneously yielding both non-quantized and quantized model variants.
  • Available now in two sizes—1 Billion and 3 Billion parameters—each size comes in both base and instruction-tuned models.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In this blogpost, we present the key highlights and rationales about the Falcon-Edge series - a collection of powerful, universal, and fine-tunable language models available in ternary format, based on the BitNet architecture.

Drawing from our experience with BitNet, Falcon-Edge introduces and validates an newly introduced pre-training paradigm that delivers a full-scope output from a single training process, simultaneously yielding both non-quantized and quantized model variants. This comprehensive approach produces a non-BitNet model in bfloat16 format, the native BitNet model, and a pre-quantized BitNet variant specifically engineered for effortless fine-tuning, enabling people and developers to precisely tailor these models to their specific applications and needs.

Available now in two sizes—1 Billion and 3 Billion parameters—each size comes in both base and instruction-tuned models. Discover the Falcon-Edge series on our dedicated Hugging Face collection.

According to recent reports, large Language Models (LLMs), by design, are inherently large and resource-intensive. As demand grows to deploy these models efficiently on edge devices, research into model compression has accelerated. Recent efforts, such as those by DeepSeek and Llama 4, explore training with reduced precision formats—down to FP8—to improve deployment scalability. On the other hand, many state-of-the-art methods emphasize post-training quantization. In contrast to these approaches, BitNet introduces a fundamentally different paradigm: unlike reduced-precision training which still relies on floating-point formats, and post-training quantization which adjusts weights after full-precision training, BitNet operates with the lowest possible precision — ternary weights ({-1, 0, 1}) — directly during training, enabling an end-to-end ultra-efficient model design.

Industry observers note that these ternary weights are paving the way for a “matmul-free” LLM design that is notably faster and remarkably memory-efficient in practice. The primary challenge of this innovative approach is the necessity for pre-training BitNet models, which can be computationally demanding and costly for typical consumers.

Leveraging the learnings from pre-training data strategies from our center, we pre-train our model on an internal data mixture for approximately 1.5 Tera Tokens. We use the classic WSD learning rate scheduler for pre-training.

We evaluate our models (base and instruct versions) on the former Hugging Face leaderboard v2 benchmark and report the normalized results below in comparison with other models of similar size:.

Additional results (leaderboard v1) on comparing our instructed models with Microsoft’s latest BitNet model:.

Falcon-Edge demonstrates on-par and better performances than models of comparable sizes on the leaderboard v2 tasks, demonstrating that it is possible to train powerful BitNet models on desired domains while being competitive enough on other tasks.

Industry observers note that the normalization activation_norm_quant quantizes the activations in int8 format, then the activation is computed back in half precision by diving it by x_scale. Since the model has been trained with fake 8-bit activation quantization, we argue that it is possible to approximate that:.

Therefore, instead of quantizing the model post-training, injecting the weight scale after quantizing the weights should lead to a good enough “approximation” of the non-BitNet version of the model:.

We confirm this by running end-to-end evaluations on the bfloat16 variant of our 1B and 3B base models and below are the results:.

The bfloat16 counterparts of the models can be loaded directly via Hugging Face transformers by passing revision="bfloat16" in the from_pretrained function:.

It has been revealed that to the best of our knowledge, except from the most recent release from Microsoft previous BitNet releases only focus on releasing the final quantized model, making it usable only for inference. Similarly to the release from Microsoft, we propose to extend the accessibility of research and application of BitNet models by releasing their pre-quantized weights. That way, owners can either perform fine-tuning on their target domain, or do continuous pre-training of the BitNet checkpoint as long as nn.Linear layers are replaced by BitnetLinear layers, and by making sure to quantize the model post training in BitNet format. Since the weights corresponds to the pre-quantized weights, performing text generation without replacing the nn.Linear layers with BitnetLinear layers will produce gibberish output.

The pre-quantized weights can be downloaded via Hugging Face's transformers library by specifying the revision argument to be prequantized:.

It has been revealed that this way, we will help fostering an ecosystem around first powerful 1-bit fine-tunes by the community. We provide to community the tools to get easily started and fine-tune their own version of powerful BitNet models by packaging all needed utility methods for performing fine-tuning on the pre-quantized weights on a Python package called onebitllms that we will cover in the next section.

In this release, we also introduce onebitllms - a lightweight Python package that can be plugged into your favorite LLM fine-tuning tools in order to fine-tune any pre-quantized BitNet model. At this time of writing onebitllms exposes these main functionalities:.

Currently, only full-finetuning is supported through this framework, while in this release the model sizes are relatively small, supporting Parameter-Efficient Fine-tuning (PEFT) methods for BitNet models remains an exciting and impactful open question for upcoming BitNet models.

To get started, simply install the package directly through pip or from source, and take a look at examples/ folders inside the source code.

With this package, we hope to accelerate research and development around ternary format LLMs, and hope to see many derivations of Falcon-Edge and other future powerful BitNet models developed by the community.

Breaking: America’s next quantum breakthrough: The factory floor

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1822 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fastcompany

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Building a quantum computing organization has taught me something that wasn’t always obvious to me as a scientist.
  • Building a quantum computing company has taught me something that wasn’t always obvious to me as a scientist.
  • Sources indicate that for years, the prevailing wisdom in technology was to focus on what you do best and outsource the rest.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Building a quantum computing organization has taught me something that wasn’t always obvious to me as a scientist. Developing a upcoming technology is one challenge. Figuring out how to manufacture it reliably, at scale, is another. And the second can be every bit as difficult as the first. For years, the prevailing wisdom in technology was to focus on what you do best and outsource the rest. It made good business sense. Building manufacturing capacity is expensive, complicated, and often far removed from the work that inspired someone to start a technology company in the first place. But that approach comes with a tradeoff. When you depend on someone else to manufacture your technology, you also depend on their capabilities, priorities, and timelines. For an emerging industry like quantum information, those dependencies can become significant obstacles. And I believe they have implications well beyond any one company. A LESSON WE’VE ALREADY LEARNED The United States has seen what happens when technological innovation and manufacturing become separated. American companies designed many of the advanced semiconductors powering today’s AI revolution, but much of the manufacturing capacity needed to produce them was developed overseas. That arrangement supported decades of innovation and economic growth. It also created dependencies that have become increasingly difficult to ignore. Now, the U.S. is investing heavily in rebuilding domestic semiconductor manufacturing capacity. It’s a difficult and expensive undertaking, and one that will take years to fully realize. Quantum technologies give us an opportunity to think about these challenges earlier in an industry’s development. The U.S. has extraordinary strengths in quantum science. Our universities, national laboratories, and private companies have helped advance the field for decades. But the path from a scientific breakthrough to a useful product requires more than research. Much more. It requires specialized materials, fabrication processes, engineering expertise, and the ability to produce increasingly complex technologies consistently and economically. Those capabilities need to develop alongside science. WHY WE CHOSE TO BUILD I’ve experienced this challenge firsthand at Quantum Computing Inc. Our work in quantum photonics depends on highly specialized manufacturing processes. As we developed our technology, we had to think carefully about how much of our future we wanted to depend on outside manufacturing partners. For a growing company, investing in your own manufacturing capabilities is a consequential decision. It requires capital, specialized expertise, and a willingness to take on responsibilities that extend well beyond research and product development. We ultimately decided to build and acquire manufacturing capacity because we believe greater control over the critical and proprietary processes is essential to our long-term strategy. For other processes, we will leverage existing manufacturing capabilities and collaborate with industry partners to build a robust, reliable, and sustainable supply chain. We also see an opportunity to contribute to the broader ecosystem by making our manufacturing capabilities available to others. The quantum opportunity is far bigger than any one company. Advancing the industry will require collaboration and shared capabilities that benefit all of us. It’s time to work together to build that foundation and accelerate the growth of the quantum industry. NO ONE MANUFACTURING MODEL That decision has shaped how I think about innovation. When researchers and engineers have closer access to manufacturing, they can learn from what happens during fabrication and use that knowledge to improve the next design. Manufacturing becomes part of the development process itself. The experience gained along the way can be just as valuable as the equipment. There is no single manufacturing model that makes sense for every quantum company. Different technologies have different requirements, and outside foundries and specialized partners remain notable. But access to reliable manufacturing capacity can have a profound influence on how rapidly an idea becomes something useful. BUILD AN INDUSTRY, NOT JUST A TECHNOLOGY Washington D.C. is beginning to recognize this challenge. A June executive order addressing quantum technology calls for strengthening domestic manufacturing capabilities and expanding partnerships between government and private industry. I welcome that attention. But building a manufacturing base requires more than funding announcements and policy commitments. It takes facilities, equipment, specialized talent, and years of experience developing processes that work consistently. It also requires demand from companies that are ready to move technologies out of the laboratory and into practical use. Other countries recognize the importance of these capabilities, with many having committed substantial resources to quantum technology. The United States has important advantages in research, entrepreneurship, and private investment. We should be building on those strengths now. That doesn’t mean every component needs to be manufactured domestically. International partnerships and global supply chains will continue to play important roles. But we should be deliberate about which capabilities are essential to our technological independence, making sure we have the capacity to develop and sustain them. FINAL THOUGHTS I’ve spent much of my career working to advance quantum technology. Like many scientists, I was initially drawn to the possibilities of what we could discover and what those discoveries make possible. Today, I spend just as much time thinking about what it takes to turn those possibilities into something people can use. That means manufacturing, supply chains, engineering, and all the difficult work that follows a breakthrough. The U.S. has an extraordinary foundation in quantum science. What we do with that advantage now matters. We need to invest in the ability to manufacture these technologies with the same conviction and intensity we brought to discovering them. Yuping Huang is CEO of Quantum Computing Inc.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The official movie poster for Artificial, Luca Guadagnino’s upcoming film about OpenAI, looks like AI slop, only it was drawn by human hands. Anyone who has come across AI-generated images knows they often carry telltale mistakes. So when film studio Neon released the poster this week, people on social media were quick to catch oddities in the illustration, leading some to suspect it was made using AI. At first glance, the poster looks normal. On a closer look, Andrew Garfield, who plays Sam Altman in the movie, doesn’t appear quite like himself, lingering somewhere in the uncanny valley. The background features San Francisco’s landscape, except the Golden Gate Bridge is underwater. The tree behind Garfield looks distorted, with a Pinocchio-like face surfacing from the trunk. The branches are no less strange, morphing into snakes. The closer you look, the weirder it gets. Today at the Microsoft Build conference, Satya Nadella revealed an expanded collaboration with Hugging Face, to make its wide diversity of open models easy to deploy on Azure secure infrastructure.

Industry observers note that if you head over to Azure AI Foundry today, you will find a vastly expanded collection of 10,000+ Hugging Face models you can deploy in a couple clicks to power AI applications working with text, audio and images. And we’re just getting started!

2 years ago, Microsoft and Hugging Face started a collaboration to make open models more easily accessible on Azure - back then the Hub was home to 200,000 open models.

According to recent reports, with now close to 2 million open models on Hugging Face, covering a wide diversity of tasks, modalities, domains and languages, it was time to take our collaboration to the next level. The new collaboration declared today creates a framework for mutual success to vastly expand how Azure customers can benefit from Hugging Face.

"Open source is how AI moves faster—with transparency, choice, and community at its core. This collaboration represents our commitment to that momentum. By combining Hugging Face’s vibrant model ecosystem with Azure’s secure, enterprise-grade infrastructure, we’re giving developers the freedom to pick the best model for the job—and helping organizations innovate safely and at scale.”.

-- Asha Sharma, Corporate Vice President at Microsoft.

Making more open models easily accessible to Azure customers, for secure deployment alongside tech giant private data, will enable enterprises to build AI applications and agents while being fully in control of their technology and data.

We’re enabling companies to take control of their AI destiny, deploying the best open models securely within their Azure account, to build AI applications they can trust and verify.

-- Clement Delangue, CEO and cofounder at Hugging Face.

Let’s head over to Azure AI Foundry, and select the Model Catalog. Here you can now find over 10,000 models under the Hugging Face Collection.

Models in the Collection include the most popular, trending models on Hugging Face for a wide range of tasks to work with text, audio and images - including text generation, feature extraction, fill-mask, translation, identifying sentence similarity, image classification, image segmentation, text to image generation, image to text conversion, automatic speech recognition and audio-classification.

To make the Hugging Face Collection on Azure AI Foundry enterprise-ready, we are only featuring models:.

In addition, Microsoft and Hugging Face will continuously test inference containers for vulnerabilities to maintain and patch them as needed.

Now let’s say you want to deploy for instance the popular Microsoft Phi-4 Reasoning Plus open model.

First, let’s select the model in the Hugging Face Collection in Azure AI Foundry, and click the “Deploy button”. The form allows you to select a VM, instance count and deployment parameters, and start the deployment process with just another click!

Now, if you prefer browsing models on the Hub, you can also start from the model page - the “Deploy on Azure ML” option will take you to the same deployment option within Azure AI Machine Learning Studio.

We are really excited about all the new Hugging Face models and modalities now directly available within Azure AI Foundry, but we’re not going to stop there!

In the weeks and months to come, you can expect a rolling thunder of updates:.

If you’re on Azure, it’s time to build with open models!

#34867. Industry News: AI adoption could disproportionately harm Black and Latino workers

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1106 w)

Industry News: AI adoption could disproportionately harm Black and Latino workers

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1106 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fastcompany

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that it has become increasingly clear that the AI revolution is not just poised to upend white-collar jobs, despite what public discourse might suggest.
  • It has become increasingly clear that the AI revolution is not just poised to upend white-collar jobs, despite what public discourse might suggest.
  • The effects of this upheaval will be uneven, which means certain demographic groups are more likely to be impacted.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that it has become increasingly clear that the AI revolution is not just poised to upend white-collar jobs, despite what public discourse might suggest. While entry-level roles are, in fact, on the decline in tech and finance—and employers continue to use AI as a rationale for layoffs—there is ample evidence that rapid AI adoption could interrupt pathways for workers without college degrees. The effects of this upheaval will be uneven, which means certain demographic groups are more likely to be impacted. Some of the jobs that have been deemed “highly exposed” to AI, including clerical and administrative roles, are largely dominated by women, and a latest report from the McKinsey Institute for Economic Mobility posits that Black and Latino workers could also face major consequences. The report finds that Black and Latino workers are overrepresented in the sectors where automation and AI adoption will supplant work altogether, rather than augment work. While the overall rate of AI adoption is relatively stable across different demographics, Black and Latino workers will be affected more acutely by job displacement. Across working hours that are impacted by AI adoption, 40% of hours performed by Black workers and 41% by Latino workers will be displaced (as compared to 37% among white workers). That may not seem like a huge gap. But as the report points out, many of the jobs that are most exposed to AI have historically been pathways to the middle class, making them crucial drivers of social mobility across communities that have faced systemic barriers to entry. Black workers, in particular, dominate six jobs that are likely to see the biggest decline in labor demand, according to McKinsey, including postal mail carriers and customer service representatives; Latino workers are also especially likely to hold some of those jobs, namely dishwashers and hand packers. Black and Latino workers—along with workers in rural regions—are also much more likely to be in jobs that involve physical labor, which are more vulnerable to being automated through robotics and other AI-enabled systems. On the whole, lower-wage workers will face the greatest impact, and are 7.6 times as likely to need to transition into a new job when compared to higher-wage workers; people without a college degree are 1.8 times more likely to need to do the same. Meanwhile, white workers are better positioned to both avoid this level of AI disruption and actually benefit from AI adoption in a number of ways. It’s not just that they’re more likely to hold jobs where AI will enhance their work, boosting productivity rather than replacing employees outright. When compared to their Black and Latino counterparts, white workers are also 30% to 50% more likely to work in the industries where private capital will be deployed, yielding more jobs and wealth creation, the McKinsey report states. That means white workers already have more of a foothold in jobs involving robotics or semiconductors or biotech, setting them up for success as hundreds of billions of dollars pour into those industries. (Look no further than the Anthropic IPO this week, which has created thousands of millionaires.)  In other words: Without broader policy changes or reskilling initiatives, many Black and Latino workers may be forced out of their jobs and locked out of opportunities to cash in on the AI boom.

He also got the vain people of the Capitol to feel for Katniss and Peeta and send them life-saving supplies, such as medicine and water. Plan, collaborate, and adapt Managers will have to work with many different personalities, departments, or vendors. True leaders can approach each individual or organization in a way that uplifts their strengths. All this planning doesn’t mean the man can’t adapt. He thrives under pressure. He was the victor of the 50th Hunger Games, the Second Quarter Quell. He had to compete against 47 other tributes, double the usual amount. He won by using the force field around the arena against his opponent. In business, as in the Hunger Games, not everything is going to go according to the five-year-plan. Sometimes you have to improvise solutions as problems arise. Sunrise will reveal more of Abernathy’s story and administrative prowess. The business world should take note.

For most developers and freelancers, all of it lives in Google Workspace or Microsoft 365. Both are excellent tools, and both encrypt your data in transit and at rest. But in their standard setup, the provider holds the encryption keys, which means your provider (and the integrated apps and AI features connected to it) can access what's inside.

Proton Workspace takes a different approach: the same everyday tools, with encryption designed so that not even Proton can read your data.

Here's how the three compare, what each does best, and which makes the most sense for how you work.

Google and Microsoft are built around ecosystem integration. Proton is built around keeping your data yours, without sacrificing productivity tools.

In a recent development, google Workspace is the go-to suite for startups, agencies and freelancers, and for good reason. Gmail, Drive, Docs, Sheets, Calendar and Meet work together seamlessly, and several people can edit the same file in real time without emailing versions back and forth.

In a recent development, google encrypts data at rest and in transit, and offers client-side encryption on eligible editions. But that extra layer requires higher-tier plans and configuration, so in the default experience Google holds the keys. A password manager and VPN aren't part of the suite.

Best for: Teams whose top priorities are real-time collaboration and third-party integrations.

If your work runs on Word, Excel and Outlook, Microsoft 365 needs little introduction. Business Standard includes full desktop apps, and Excel remains the benchmark for heavy spreadsheet work.

That breadth comes with complexity. Licensing, permissions and device management can eat into time a small team or solo developer would rather spend shipping. And like Google, Microsoft's everyday productivity experience isn't built around end-to-end encryption, while Copilot and advanced security features add cost.

Best for: Businesses built on desktop Office apps and established Microsoft workflows.

Industry observers note that proton Workspace starts from a different premise. Instead of building a productivity suite and adding privacy features on top, Proton built privacy into the foundation, then delivered the everyday tools around it.

What's included in Workspace Standard:.

Everything is managed from one admin console, with one bill.

This is the core difference. Proton uses zero-access encryption: your data is encrypted before it reaches Proton's servers, and Proton never holds the keys. Proton can't read your data. Not won't. Can't.

That has practical consequences:.

The honest trade-offs: Proton Docs and Sheets cover core editing and collaboration, not every advanced Excel feature. There's no presentation app yet, and the third-party integration ecosystem is smaller than Google's or Microsoft's.

Best for: Developers, freelancers, agencies and startups that handle client data, code and credentials, and want privacy and savings in one suite.

US prices for comparable plans with annual billing, excluding taxes:.

The headline prices are close. The real cost isn't:.

Proton Workspace covers business email, 1 TB of encrypted storage, docs, sheets, video calls, a password manager and a VPN. That's one bill instead of three.

Workspace Premium and adds 3 TB of storage per user, 20 custom domains, meetings for up to 250 participants, Lumo private AI and email data retention policies for only $7 more per month. Both prepares include a 14-day free trial, and annual plans are currently up to 20% off.

Choose Google Workspace if your team lives in real-time collaboration and relies heavily on Google's integration ecosystem.

Choose Microsoft 365 if your work depends on desktop Excel, PowerPoint and established Microsoft workflows.

Choose Proton Workspace if you handle client data, proprietary code or credentials you don't want readable by your provider or if you want privacy you can verify, with open-source, audited apps.

Is Proton Workspace a good alternative to Google Workspace for developers?

Sources indicate that yes, for developers who prioritize privacy and cost. It covers email, storage, documents, spreadsheets and video calls, adds a password manager and VPN, and costs $12.99/user/month versus $14 for Google Workspace Business Standard.

Can Google Workspace or Microsoft 365 read my email and files?

In a recent development, by default, yes. Google Workspace and Microsoft 365 hold the encryption keys, and their default terms give them access to your data.

Can Proton read my email and files?

In a recent development, no. Zero-access encryption means Proton never holds the keys to your stored data. Emails between Proton users are end-to-end encrypted automatically, and you can send password-protected encrypted emails to anyone.

Sources indicate that yes. Proton's apps are open source and independently audited.

Can I use Proton Mail with my existing email client?

Yes. Proton Mail Bridge connects Outlook, Apple Mail and Thunderbird.

Does Google Workspace or Microsoft 365 use my data to train AI?

In a recent development, it can. If your plan allows Google Workspace or Microsoft 365 to hold the encryption keys, they can access your data and use it to train their integrated AI models.

Does Proton use my data to train AI?

It has been revealed that no. Proton can't read your data, so it can't use it for AI training.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • We were inspired by Andrej Karpathy’s nanoGPT, and provide a similar project for the vision domain.
  • In a recent development, at its heart, nanoVLM is a toolkit that helps you build and train a model that can understand both images and text, and then generate text based on that.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, nanoVLM is the simplest way to get started with training your very own Vision Language Model (VLM) using pure PyTorch. It is lightweight toolkit which allows you to launch a VLM training on a free tier colab notebook.

We were inspired by Andrej Karpathy’s nanoGPT, and provide a similar project for the vision domain.

In a recent development, at its heart, nanoVLM is a toolkit that helps you build and train a model that can understand both images and text, and then generate text based on that. The beauty of nanoVLM lies in its simplicity. The entire codebase is intentionally kept minimal and readable, making it perfect for beginners or anyone who wants to peek under the hood of VLMs without getting overwhelmed.

In this blog post, we cover the core ideas behind the project and provide a simple way to interact with the repository. We not only go into the details of the project but also encapsulate all of it so that you can quickly get started.

You can start training a Vision Language Model using our nanoVLM toolkit by following these steps:.

Here is a Colab notebook that will help you launch a training run with no local setup required!

As the name suggests, a Vision Language Model (VLM) is a multi-modal model that processes two modalities: vision and text. These models typically take images and/or text as input and generate text as output.

Generating text (output) conditioned on the understanding of images and texts (inputs) is a powerful paradigm. It enables a wide range of applications, from image captioning and object detection to answering questions about visual content (as shown in the table below). One thing to note is that nanoVLM focuses only on Visual Question Answering as the training objective.

If you are interested in learning more about VLMs, we strongly recommend reading our latest blog on the topic: Vision Language Models (Better, Faster, Stronger).

"Talk is cheap, show me the code" - Linus Torvalds.

In this section, we’ll guide you through the codebase. It’s helpful to keep a tab open for reference as you follow along.

It has been revealed that below is the folder structure of our repository. We have removed helper files for brevity.

Sources indicate that we model nanoVLM after two well known and widely used architectures. Our vision backbone (models/vision_transformer.py) is the standard vision transformer, more specifically Google’s SigLIP vision encoder. Our language backbone follows the Llama 3 architecture.

In a recent development, the vision and text modalities are aligned using a Modality Projection module. This module takes the image embeddings produced by the vision backbone as input, and transforms them into embeddings compatible with the text embeddings from the embedding layer of the language model. These embeddings are then concatenated and fed into the language decoder. The Modality Projection module consists of a pixel shuffle operation followed by a linear layer.

Pixel shuffle reduces the number of image tokens, which helps reduce computational cost and speeds up training, especially for transformer-based language decoders which are sensitive to input length. The figure below demonstrates the concept.

According to recent reports, all the files are very lightweight and well documented. We highly encourage you to check them out individually to get a better understanding of the implementation details (models/xxx.py).
